messages.subject: Re: Subset of nodes not updating when using dmulti
messages.subject_clean: Subset of nodes not updating when using dmulti
messages.body_plain:
Hi Chloe and David,

Sorry, this fell by the wayside indeed during vISEC2020.

The PMCMC implementation can handle vector state dynamics.  However, if observed numbers of observable states are error-free, then particle filtering methods can be problematic because the chance of a simulation hitting the observations can be low.  I am not sure if that is the case.

I do have ideas about samplers for the model with multinomial state dynamics.  While we like to keep discussions general and open on the list, I wonder if this will involve extended discussion of a somewhat narrow topic and is best taken off-list.  We can report back for interested list readers later.

-Perry

On Mon, Jun 22, 2020 at 6:46 AM Chloe Nater <gani...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Hi again Perry!
>
> Thank you very much for looking into this. All of us (David from above, me, and you) seem to agree about where the problem is most likely coming from, and it does look like solving it will require to write a custom sampler that works on autocorrelated multinomial nodes, i.e. does not condition on the size argument.
> I think having such a sampler would be useful not just for me and this specific problem, but also for other users (working with more complex population models, and possibly other kinds of models as well), and I would very much like to give it a try.
>
> While my knowledge of MCMC samplers is rather limited at the moment, I am keen on learning more.
> Would you - or other members of the NIMBLE team - be interested in helping me with this, at least in the beginning? Would be happy to chat, as it's also ISEC at the moment!
> (Any pointers towards relevant literature and/or examples to get started would be much appreciated too!)
>
> Cheers,
>
> Chloé
>
> On Monday, 22 June 2020 02:30:35 UTC+2, pdevalpine wrote:
> > Hi Chloe,
> >
> > I've given this a little more thought.  I think I see the purpose of how you have set things up.  Unfortunately, it does not seem like an easy problem to solve. The current dmulti sampler conditions on size.  I think an update at one step could make the next step impossible by creating a mismatch between the size of the dmulti and the resulting states.  For example, if N[z, 1:9, t] is updated in a way that moves some individuals from alive states to dead states, then sum(N[1:3, z, t]) will no longer match the sum of the random variable it defines, namely sum(N[z, 1:9, t+1]).  I don't know if you've made any progress reformulating the model based on the twitter thread.  I imagine it would be possible to sample this model with a custom sampler that respects the constraints involved.   I don't think a vanilla block sampler will work.
> >
> > -Perry
> >
> >
> > On Fri, Jun 19, 2020 at 1:03 AM Chloe Nater <gani...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > That's fantastic news, thank you very much Perry. Let me know if I can assist in any way.
> > >
> > > Chloé
> > >
> > >
> > > On Thursday, 18 June 2020 16:15:18 UTC+2, pdevalpine wrote:
> > > > Hi Chloe,
> > > >
> > > > I agree we should be able to solve this with appropriate samplers, rather than your having to rewrite the model.  We're going to look at the multinomial sampler.
> > > >
> > > > -Perry
> > > >
> > > > On Thu, Jun 18, 2020 at 4:49 AM Chloe Nater <gani...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > Hi David!
> > > > >
> > > > > Thank you very much for your reply, this makes a lot of sense.
> > > > > It also explains why I only got this issue when using the multinomial likelihood with a "size" that is estimated (when "size" is a fixed constant, i.e. given as data, there was no problem).
> > > > >
> > > > > I am now wondering what would be the best way to go about circumventing this problem.
> > > > > From my view, this can be approached either by changing the samplers, or changing the model structure.
> > > > >
> > > > > Samplers:
> > > > > I assume none of the other "pre-programmed" samplers in the r-nimble package would be able to deal with this? Could there be a solution involving block sampling?
> > > > > Surely, some samplers for autoregressive multinomial likelihoods must have been developed? Is anyone aware of examples?
> > > > > I would greatly appreciate any pointers towards already existing solutions, or for building a custom sampler to deal with this.
> > > > >
> > > > > Model structure:
> > > > > Alternatively, getting rid of the autoregressive multinomial likelihood may solve the problem.
> > > > > The obvious way of doing this seems to be rewriting the model as sequential (and conditional) binomial likelihoods. However, this is not just inelegant, but kind of defeats the purpose of what we would like to do with this model in practice ("general" integrated population model allowing for >2 transitions conditional on survival).
> > > > > Are there any alternative formulations for the model that I may not be thinking of at the moment?
> > > > >
> > > > > Any thoughts, ideas, and references (from anyone!) very welcome!
> > > > >
> > > > > Cheers,
> > > > >
> > > > > Chloé
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >

messages.subject: Use simulate() to generate samples from a truncated distribution
messages.subject_clean: Use simulate() to generate samples from a truncated distribution
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am wondering whether it is possible to use the simulate() function to generate samples from a truncated distribution...

The code for the model is below... I am trying to model birth and death ages that follow a specific custom distribution (which I dont have a quantile function for).
I have a mixture of left/right and interval censored data for both births and deaths, the model runs fine but I then want to do some model comparisons for which I need to simulate death times from the truncated distribution... once I have defined the model (nimbleModel) I can pull out the generated tD values which is fine but if I then try to use simulate$tD then the next set of values provided ignore the truncation limits, they are just from the custom distribution.

So is it possible to keep simulating more death ages but use the truncated distribution from the limits that I have from the data??

I hope that makes sense... many thanks

Dave

tB - birth date
tD - death date

code <- nimbleCode({

  ## survival components for dead badgers
  for (i in 1:nind) {

    ## likelihood for interval-truncated distribution
    censoredB[i] ~ dinterval(tB[i], cintB[i, ])
    tB[i] ~ dflat()
    censoredD[i] ~ dinterval(tD[i], cintD[i, ])
    tD[i] ~ cdist(a1, a2, b1, b2, c, tB[i])

    ## sampling component
    nm[i] <- max(ceiling(tB[i]), 0)
    nM[i] <- min(floor(tD[i]) - nm[i], tMax - nm[i])
    pd[i] <- exp(y[i] * log(mean.p) + (nM[i] - y[i]) * log(1 - mean.p))
    dind[i] ~ dbern(pd[i])

  ## priors
  a1 ~ dexp(1)
  a2 ~ dexp(1)
  b1 ~ dexp(1)
  b2 ~ dexp(1)
  c ~ dexp(1)
  mean.p ~ dunif(0, 1)

})

## set up other components of model
consts <- list(nind = nind, tMax = ncol(CH))
data <- list(y = y, cintB = cintB, cintD = cintD,
             censoredB = censoredB, censoredD = censoredD,
             tD = tD, tB = tB, dind = dind, constraint_data = constraint_data)

## set initial values
tBinit <- apply(cbind(cintB, censoredB), 1, function(x) {
  if(x[3] == 0) {
    y <- x[1] - rexp(1, 0.1)
  } else {
    y <- runif(1, x[1], x[2])
  }
  y
})
tDinit <- apply(cbind(cintD, censoredD), 1, function(x) {
  if(x[3] == 2) {
    y <- x[2] + rexp(1, 0.1)
  } else {
    y <- runif(1, x[1], x[2])
  }
  y
})
inits <- list(
  tD = tDinit,
  tB = tBinit,
  a1 = 0.1,
  a2 = 0.1,
  b1 = 0.1,
  b2 = 0.1,
  mean.p = runif(1, 0, 1),
  c = 0.05
)

messages.body_plain:
To follow up on this on the list (after an exchange between Mike and
me off-list), if you use dinterval, e.g.,

for(i in 1:n)
  y_cens[i] ~ dinterval(y[i], c[i])

Then `y_cens` should be specified as 'data'. If you specify it as
'constants', nimble will convert to 'data' behind the scenes.

'c' can be specified either constants if the values of 'c' are indeed
fixed. If 'c' has a prior, then one would specify its values via
'inits'.
If 'c' only appears on the right-hand side (i.e., it has no prior) but
you may want to change the values, you can specify its values either
via 'inits' or 'data'.

-Chris

On Mon, Jun 29, 2020 at 7:40 PM MIke Sparago <mikes...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> I attempted to confirm that the dinterval() censored data vector should be treated as constants vs. data, since we (apparently) got higher ESS when making that change. I ran our model, which has a large proportion of censored data 10 times and calculated the min efficiency for both cases. These results (shown below) indicate that there is no significant difference in efficiency with the censoring vector as constants vs. data. I would have to retrace our steps again, but perhaps we had a change in initial values that caused our ESS improvement. We are currently close in ESS between JAGS and NIMBLE, but as you can see the MCMC efficiency is low.

> On Thursday, June 25, 2020 at 10:30:04 AM UTC-4, MIke Sparago wrote:
>>
>> Daniel / Perry,
>>
>> We appear to have resolved the problem, with your help of course.  After I responded to Perry's post, where I indicated that a large proportion of our data is censored, it occurred to me that the censoring vector (from dinterval) was treated as data, as opposed to constants.  Moving the censoring vector to constants brought the ESS much closer to JAGS.  Once that was completed, blocking improvements were also more successful.  Additionally, we saw ESS improvements when providing a better initial value for one parameter.  As Perry indicated, the slice sampler warnings disappeared after the initial value was improved for that parameter.
>>
>> Daniel's suggestion to use 'onlySlice = TRUE' did indeed increase the ESS,  but significantly increased the runtime, as expected.
>>
>> I feel like we have a good starting point now, and can work toward further MCMC improvements.
>>
>> Thanks, Mike
>>
>> On Wednesday, June 24, 2020 at 8:33:09 PM UTC-4, MIke Sparago wrote:
>>>
>>> Thanks for the chime, Perry. My model is fully initialized and I am using the same initialization function with both NIMBLE and JAGS. Still, I will review the initial values, as you suggested.
>>>
>>> I was thinking of posting a minimal example, but would need to simplify the model before doing so. Although it is not as advanced as some of your ecological models, I do not consider it a simple GLM, with 1,305 observed stochastic nodes, 2,430 unobserved stochastic nodes and a graph size of 35.564. Perhaps the real answer is that we need to work on the parameterization.
>>>
>>> We are working with NIMBLE because there are opportunities with user-defined distributions that we need to explore, so we're not ready to give up yet.
>>>
>>> On Wednesday, June 24, 2020 at 7:42:28 PM UTC-4, pdevalpine wrote:
>>>>
>>>> Hi Mike,
>>>>
>>>> Let me chime in with a couple of notes.
>>>>
>>>> It is more important for NIMBLE than for JAGS to provide sensible and complete inits.  If you are not doing that, it could explain some degree of worse performance of NIMBLE.  That could be one source of the slice sampler warnings you saw.
>>>>
>>>> It is also important to recognize there are relatively simple special cases where JAGS is at its best relative to NIMBLE, and simple lms and glms may potentially be those cases, anecdotally.
>>>>
>>>> -Perry
>>>>
>>>> On Wed, Jun 24, 2020 at 2:56 PM MIke Sparago <mikes...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>>>>
>>>>> Thanks for your reply, Daniel.  I attended the recent NIMBLE workshop and recall the discussion about MCMC efficiency.  As far as a 'best practice', we have traditionally adopted the guidance found in Kruschke's book and blog, where he suggests an ESS of at least 10,000. Certainly, the diagnostics plots look convincing with multiple chains at that level of ESS, which helps to sell the approach to those less familiar Bayesian modeling.  I will take another look at MCMC efficiency as a metric going forward.
>>>>>
>>>>> Regarding your suggestion of using 'onlySlice = TRUE', I am in the process of testing, but am seeing Warnings for "slice sampler reached maximum number of contractions" for several parameters, with current parameter values on the order of 1E+16.  I will see if there is any improvement when the MCMC has completed.  Thanks again.
>>>>>
>>>>>
>>>>> On Wednesday, June 24, 2020 at 4:33:49 PM UTC-4, Daniel Turek wrote:
>>>>>>
>>>>>> Mike, when you configure the MCMC, usually a step using configureMCMC(), you could try adding the option:
>>>>>> configureMCMC(model, onlySlice = TRUE)
>>>>>>
>>>>>> This will assign slice samplers for all non-conjugate scalar nodes in your model, very nearly replicating (with a few possible exceptions) the sampler assignments used by JAGS.
>>>>>>
>>>>>> That said; it's not *all* about ESS.  The slice sampling will (generally) give higher ESS, but at the expense of a longer MCMC runtime.  We usually consider "MCMC efficiency" (which we define as min(ESS) / runtime, where the min() is taken across the sampled parameters) as the metric of how well an MCMC is doing, because that truly reflects how large an ESS you can generate, per unit runtime of MCMC sampling (for the slowest mixing model parameter).

messages.body_plain:
Hi Keith,

a) In general, it would be surprising that using a user-defined nimbleFunction is slower than having the calculation as part of your model directly.
However, if using the nimbleFunction causes an increase in the number of dependencies when updating a given parameter, it could slow things down. I think that may be happening here - in the version without a nimbleFunction, if you update t[1] then only some of the nu and p values need to be recalculated. But with the nimbleFunction, all of the nu and p values are recalculated.

Also, given 'point' is only 3, we wouldn't expect using a nimbleFunction to help much even if there wasn't the question of changing the number of dependencies.

b) I'm not sure how you would avoid the intermediate calculation, given that 'p' is a function of 't', 'tau', and 'alpha'. I may be misunderstanding what you are asking.

-chris

hi Keith,

a) I didn't take the time to see all of what is going on with dependencies, but my general comment still holds -- you want to write your model (and associated user-defined nimbleFunctions) in such a way that you avoid unnecessary dependencies. It looks like there are distinct parameters for each pair of {n,i} values that determine the likelihood for res[n,i]. Alternatively, if you do introduce additional dependencies, it may make sense to do block sampling.

b) You could write a user-defined distribution that both calculates 'p' and does the dcat calculation all at the same time, thereby avoiding having all the 'p' nodes.

-chris

messages.subject: Re: Large memory demands by WAIC calculation
messages.subject_clean: Large memory demands by WAIC calculation
messages.body_plain:
Hi Vincent,

I'll mention you can calculate WAIC after running the MCMC chains. As Chris described, you need a matrix of likelihoods, one row per iteration (all chains combined), and one column per datum. This is easy to calculate, as you basically just "reverse" the BUGS code you wrote to calculate the likelihoods (but in R). You can then use waic() in the loo package to calculate WAIC.  I've been doing this to avoid the same memory problems you mentioned.

Adam

On Monday, June 29, 2020 at 1:03:42 PM UTC-5 vin...@csp-inc.org wrote:
> Ah, great to know! I will thin for sure. I misunderstood the docs wrt thinning and WAIC. I got mixed up when reading about the burnin option for WAIC not accounting for thinning, and I incorrectly thought that WAIC ignored thinning entirely. I'll test this out for now. Thanks!
>
> On Monday, June 29, 2020 at 10:18:33 AM UTC-6 christophe...@gmail.com wrote:
> > Hi Vincent,
> >
> > In calculating WAIC (which involves calculating predictive density values) we fill a matrix with a row for each MCMC sample and a column for each data point. With the number of iterations you have and the number of data points, this can use a lot of memory.
> >
> > I doubt you need to save that many iterations to get a good posterior summary or a robust WAIC estimate, so you might want to thin your MCMC output to save on memory in this case, if you are running out of memory.
> >
> > I believe we could modify our WAIC calculation to not store all those predictive density values at the same time, but it would be a bit involved because the current calculation tries to be careful about avoiding numerical underflow to ensure numerical stability. There are lots of models with as much or more data as you have, so we should try to make the WAIC work such that it doesn't use up so much memory. I'll make a note for us to look into this, though it's not something we'll likely get to in the very near term.
> >
> > -chris

Thanks for the question.  The rank function is not built in.  Some options would be to write it as a user-defined function (nimbleFunction -- see User Manual), to do posterior prediction as a post-processing step (unless you need to reduce the size of what is monitored for mcmc output, and the monitors2/thin2 doesn't help), or to use min and/or max if they can help you get what you want.  If you get stuck trying to write a user-defined function, please feel free to post another question saying how you want it to work (I think JAGS and WinBUGS have different rank functions, so it would be easiest if you say for sure what you want).

-Perry

messages.body_plain:
Hi Diego,

Thanks for sharing with sufficient detail to see what is going on.

Can you please try the following:

Add returnType(double(1)) in the run function of Sort.Func.  That's a return type declaration (a numeric vector) so it is not evaluated as a line of code and can go anywhere.

Change the use in model code to:
sort.b.Fac[1:facility]<-Sort.Func(b.Facility[1:facility])
(outside the for loop)

Since you are returning a vector, it needs to be assigned to a vector.  If you want to pick out a scalar, it would be better to pass i as an argument to Sort.Fun and use returnType(double(0)) to return a scalar (rather than pick it out with [i] later, which I'm not sure will work but might).

For efficiency, non-scalars in compiled code are passed by reference.  This is very un-R-like.  In your case, you will want to copy X in Sort.Func before sorting it.

Model nodes cannot change size, so X<-X[!is.na <http://is.na>(X)] may be problematic if you do not know in advance how large the intended return object is.  It might work well to keep the return object the same length as X and put any NAs at the end.

In your previous message, I may not have followed, but it looked like maybe you wanted to use the ranked() idea to get the smallest and largest values.  If that's the case, min or max would work.

I hope that gets you closer to what you need.

-Perry

messages.body_plain:
Hi Diego,

Thanks for continuing with this.  There are several things going on.  In a nutshell, the compiler doesn't currently support NA very thoroughly.  This has come up in a couple of contexts recently, so I have drafted better support for it and have a draft pull request on our GitHub repository, which is running our test suite at the moment.

One reason we haven't supported NA very deeply through the compiler is that, in a model, it's not clear whether one really wants to be handling NAs in functions and distributions.  A common role for NAs has been to mark missing data when creating a model, which one wants to be sampled via MCMC, so that during MCMC operation the values are not actually NAs.  If there are NAs permanently in place in other variables in a model, often one would work around them in the model code, such as by using nested indexing to exclude any cases with NAs.  You probably have a good reason for wanting to handle them, but it might be worth thinking about avoiding them entirely.

If you do need to use NAs and want to do it in your own code similar to Sort.Func, what I suggest at the moment is establishing a protocol to use some non-possible number as your proxy for NA.  Another option would be to use NaN instead of NA.  You can assign NaN to a double (e.g. X[i] <- NaN).  Compilation does not support vectorized is.nan, so you would have to check for NaNs in the input vector (X) one by one in a for loop.  However, see below for a possibly more appealing solution.

It may be that we should add support for sort and rank for nimbleFunction compilation, but here is a way you could do it that simply calls R's C implementation of sort and thus achieves its handling of NAs, which is to put them at the end.  This is basically the same scheme as we used for the Bessel I function in another recent post on this list.  I know it is somewhat obscure to see what R's C headers expose for this kind of step, but they are in the includes directory of an R installation.  Here is the trick:

library(nimble)

sink('external_sort.h')
cat('
extern "C" {
 void R_double_sort(double *x, int n);
}
')
sink()
sink('external_sort.cpp')
cat('
 #include <R.h>
 #include "external_sort.h"
 void R_double_sort(double *x, int n) {
   R_rsort(x, n);
 }
')
sink()
system2("R", c("CMD", "SHLIB", "external_sort.cpp")) ## Ignore the .so (or .DLL).  We will use the external_sort.o
R_double_sort <- nimbleExternalCall(function(x = double(1), n = integer()) {},
                                    Cfun =  'R_double_sort',
                                    headerFile = 'external_sort.h', ## see note about paths belo2
                                    returnType = void(),
                                    oFile = 'external_sort.o')
## Because this will work by passing x by reference and having that as the sorted result,
## we need to wrap it in another layer.
nfsort <- nimbleFunction(
  run = function(x = double(1)) {
    y <- x
    R_double_sort(y, length(y))
    return(y)
    returnType(double(1))
  }
)
## Check if it works by compiling it as a stand-alone nimbleFunction
cnfsort <- compileNimble(nfsort, dirName = ".")
cnfsort(c(1, 3, 2, 5, 4)) ## It works
cnfsort(c(1, 3, NA, 5, 4)) ## It works with NA going to the end

## Use it in a model
demoCode <- nimbleCode({
  z[1:5] <- nfsort(x[1:5])
})
demoModel <- nimbleModel(demoCode, inits = list(x = c(1, 3, NA, 5, 4)),
                         check = FALSE, calculate = FALSE) ## Can't calculate in R with a nimbleExternalCall
CdemoModel <- compileNimble(demoModel, dirName = ".")
CdemoModel$z
CdemoModel$calculate("z")
CdemoModel$z
## A note about paths.  I recommend something like headerFile = normalizePath(file.path(getwd(), 'external_sort.h'))
##  and similar for oFile.
## This is important when compiling the model, which is not by default done in your local directory.
## An alternative, which I've used above, is to give local paths to hearderFile and oFile
##   and then use dirName = "." in compileNimble for the model, which makes it use your local directory
##   for the C++ files.
## On my system, this avoided problems with a space in getwd() due to "Google Drive", but those are
##   just OS details.

In summary, your two best options are: Use NaN instead of NA and do not expect vectorized behavior of is.nan(X) to work correctly.  Or use the nimbleExternalCall I've given above.

-Perry

messages.body_plain:
Hi TJ,

Thanks for the inquiry and use case.

As it happens, there was just another issue revolving around support for NA through compilation.  My response to that (a few minutes ago) may also be relevant to your need.

What it comes down to at the moment is that using a default value of NA is not going to work through compilation.  A couple of options would be to use NaN instead, to choose a protocol like -1 to indicate "NA", or to use an additional argument that is a logical to take the role of the is.na <http://is.na>(zU).

Incidentally, I don't totally follow that you have a zU in pmyexp and a zU in rmyexp that is passed as the q argument to pmyexp.  You probably have the logic worked out but that seemed potentially confusing in trying to read your code.

HTH.

-Perry

messages.subject: Speed-up a model with Dirichlet processes involved
messages.subject_clean: Speed-up a model with Dirichlet processes involved
messages.body_plain:
Hi All!

First of all, thank you for such an amazing tool as NIMBLE!

I am working with gene expression data and trying to fit a model that involves 2 Dirichlet processes.
Essentially I am assuming that gene expression is distributed according to Negative Binomial distribution, particularly, this parametric from is used (often used in genetics): https://mc-stan.org/docs/2_20/functions-reference/nbalt.html. I assume that both parameters (on log-scale) are dependent on some covariates (X1,X2...). So it is essentially like a GLM but with covariates used for both parameters. I am trying to cluster the coefficient of this linear combinations separately for each distribution parameter and this is why I am using 2 separate Dirichlet processes.

The model code is the following:
modelCode <- nimbleCode({
  #### DP
  # for mean
  for(i in 1:(H-1)){
    v[i] ~ dbeta(1, alpha)
  }
  w[1:H] <- stick_breaking(v[1:(H-1)])

  #for phi
  for(i in 1:(HH-1)){
    vv[i] ~ dbeta(1, alpha2)
  }
  ww[1:HH] <- stick_breaking(vv[1:(HH-1)])

  ### sample from G0
  # mean
  for(h in 1:H){
    a0[h] ~ dnorm(0.0,1.5)
    a1[h] ~ ddexp(0.0,1.5)
    a2[h] ~ ddexp(0.0,1.5)
    a3[h] ~ ddexp(0.0,1.5)
    a4[h] ~ ddexp(0.0,1.5)
  }
  # phi
  for(hh in 1:HH){
    b0[hh] ~ dnorm(0.0,1.5)
    b1[hh] ~ ddexp(0.0,1.5)
    b2[hh] ~ ddexp(0.0,1.5)
    b3[hh] ~ ddexp(0.0,1.5)
    b4[hh] ~ ddexp(0.0,1.5)
  }

  # likelihood
  for(g in 1:G){
    # sample category: zeta[g] in [1......H], and zeta2[g] in [1...HH]
    zeta[g] ~ dcat(w[1:H])
    zeta2[g] ~ dcat(ww[1:HH])

    for(t in 1:T){
      # sample gene expression
      Y[g,t] ~ dnegbin(p[g,t],phi[g,t])

      # construct value p[g,t] in terms of mu[g,t] and phi[g,t]
      p[g,t]   <- phi[g,t]/(scale_factors[t]*exp(logmu[g,t])+phi[g,t])
      phi[g,t] <- exp(logphi[g,t])

      # we need to define logmu[g,t]
      logmu[g,t] <- a0[zeta[g]] + a1[zeta[g]] * X1[t]+ a2[zeta[g]] * X2[t] + a3[zeta[g]]* X3[t]+ a4[zeta[g]]* X4[t]

      # define phi[g,t]
      logphi[g,t] <- b0[zeta2[g]] + b1[zeta2[g]] * X1[t] + b2[zeta2[g]] * X2[t] + b3[zeta2[g]] * X3[t] + b4[zeta2[g]] * X4[t]
    }
  }
})

The data passing and model compilation happens here:
constants  <- list(G      = G,
                   H      = n_clusters_mean,
                   HH     = n_clusters_phi,
                   T      = T,
                   alpha  = concentration_mean,
                   alpha2 = concentration_phi
                   )

data       <- list(Y             = Y,
                   X1            = X1,
                   X2            = X2,
                   X3            = X3,
                   X4            = X4,
                   scale_factors = scale_factors
                   )

inits      <- list(a0     = rnorm(constants$H, 0, 1),
                   a1     = rnorm(constants$H, 0, 1),
                   a2     = rnorm(constants$H, 0, 1),
                   a3     = rnorm(constants$H, 0, 1),
                   a4     = rnorm(constants$H, 0, 1),

                   b0     = rnorm(constants$HH, 0, 1),
                   b1     = rnorm(constants$HH, 0, 1),
                   b2     = rnorm(constants$HH, 0, 1),
                   b3     = rnorm(constants$HH, 0, 1),
                   b4     = rnorm(constants$HH, 0, 1),

                   v      = rbeta(constants$H, 1, 1),
                   vv     = rbeta(constants$HH, 1, 1)
                   )

# this is R object, not C++ object
Rmodel     <- nimbleModel(modelCode,constants,data,inits)

# lets monitor just cluster assignments z, we can change samplers here
monitors   <- c("zeta","zeta2")
RmodelConf <- configureMCMC(Rmodel, monitors = monitors,thin=lag)

# create mcmc object
Rmcmc      <- buildMCMC(RmodelConf)

print("R objects created")

# compile everything in C++
Cmodel     <- compileNimble(Rmodel,showCompilerOutput = TRUE)
Cmcmc      <- compileNimble(Rmcmc,project = Cmodel,showCompilerOutput = TRUE)

print("C++ objects created")

runMCMC_samples <- runMCMC(Cmcmc, nburnin = burnin, niter = n_steps)

The model worked fine with small dataset (200 genes and 300 cells; ran for 5.5 hrs) but there were memory issues (and, as the result, it crashed on HPC; probably not enough memory was allocated) with 1000 genes and 250 cells.
In fact the true input should be around 6K-by-600, so I am wondering what can I potentially do (if anything) to speed up the process? I read another thread here, where you suggested using calculate = False for nimbleModel(). I can also use vectorized form to compute logmu and logphi. I haven't checked it yet but I am about to.

Is there anything else I can do to speed up the model and make it less memory-consuming?

Thank you for your help.

Regards,
Evgenii

Hi Evgeny,

Thanks for the message and I'm very interested to see this application.

Let me point you to my message of June 26 on this thread:
https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/nimble-users/8vaTHQoJz2M

I commented on why nimble encounters memory problems (which we hope to improve).  Then I gave a strategy for keeping large objects out of the model.  That strategy might work well for your problem.

Looking at your model, I wonder if the following would work: Vectorize logmu and logphi over t (since any change in a parameter will affect all t).  And use a vector of dummy data values to push calculation of phi[g, 1:T], p[g, 1:T] and log probabilities of y[g, 1:T] to R (or C++) using the trick I showed in the June 26 message.  Your model code would have something like:

dummy[g] ~ dCustom(logmu[g, 1:T],  logphi[g, 1:T], g ) # do the phi, p and y steps all together

All the actual values of y would live in dCustom.

This could also be done for logmu and/or logphi at a couple of levels.  You could have

logmu[g, 1:T] <- calc_logmu(a0[zeta[g]], a1[zeta[g]], etc.)

All of the values of X would live in calc_logmu.

Going further, you could store logmu itself outside the model, using another dummy variable to serve as a low-dimensional node to establish the graph relationships in the model.  This would look something like

logmu_dummy[g] <- calc_logmu(g, a0[zeta[g]], a1[zeta[g]], etc.)

where calc_logmu would have to return a value to logmu_dummy[g] that wouldn't really matter.  The actual values of logmu would be stored in R (or C++) in the same scope from where they'd be used by dCustom.

This is all something of a workaround to the scaling issues, but it is fairly straightforward to set up once you see how the pieces fit together and allows nimble to manage the model graph and MCMC system.   I'm happy to help sort it out if it's not clear how it all can fit together.

A couple of final thoughts on your model: Sampling for dcat can be inefficient because on every iteration every possible value is tried.  It would be easy to set up a sampler that for example tries one alternative or a random subset of alternatives.  Computational cost vs. mixing is hard to predict and would depend on the model.  The dcat case is a tradeoff I've been curious about. Also, you may be good with what you've written, but nimble does have Bayesian non-parametric distributions (see blog posts linked from our documentation page at r-nimble.org <http://r-nimble.org>) and they will be improved in an upcoming release.

HTH and let me know how it goes.

-Perry

messages.body_plain:
I'm not an expert on the BNP facilities offered in NIMBLE, but I think I can comment: the stick-breaking representation (as you're using), and the CRP distribution, are modelling the same Dirichlet process.  They differ in the MCMC sampling algorithms which are applied to each, automatically, by NIMBLE's MCMC.  Translating your code between these two (mathematically identical) representations is a relatively small and straight-forward exercise.  The relative performance of the different sampling algorithms, as applied to each representation, could differ, would depend on the model and the data, and is generally difficult to predict.

Changing between the stick-breaking representation and the CRP representation, the categorical distribution would persist in your model.  And Perry's comments are correct, that (in particular for a large number of categories, e.g. large values of H or HH in your code) the categorical sampler (which is applied to the categorical distribution) would become arbitrarily inefficient, in that it evaluates the posterior density for every category value (H or HH times), then samples directly from that posterior distribution.  And that you could hopefully reduce this inefficiency by writing a customized sampling strategy (a custom-written MCMC sampler), to update your categorical distributions, in a more efficient (less wasteful) manner.

Hope this helps,
Daniel

They differ in the MCMC sampling algorithms which are applied to each, automatically, by NIMBLE's MCMC.  Translating your code between these two (mathematically identical) representations is a relatively small and straight-forward exercise.  The relative performance of the different sampling algorithms, as applied to each representation, could differ, would depend on the model and the data, and is generally difficult to predict.
>
> Changing between the stick-breaking representation and the CRP representation, the categorical distribution would persist in your model. And that you could hopefully reduce this inefficiency by writing a customized sampling strategy (a custom-written MCMC sampler), to update your categorical distributions, in a more efficient (less wasteful) manner.

You may or may not need to go down the road of writing a customized sampler for your model.  It really depends on your model, whether this is worthwhile.  I would see how performance (speed and mixing) of the MCMC is sampling is, before starting with that.

But, if you do decide to look into it, then I'd suggest first reading section15.5 of the NIMBLE user's manual ("Example: writing user-defined samplers to extend NIMBLE’s MCMC engine")
https://r-nimble.org/html_manual/cha-progr-with-models.html#sec:user-samplers

messages.body_plain:
Ok, need to take a look at that chapter! Thank you, Daniel.

Perry,

I am not sure I managed to incorporate all your ideas in the code (as I did not fully understand all of the points). However, I did the following and it seemed to improve the speed. I am still wondering if additional improvement can be achieved (particularly, I am still sending count data matrix Y to NIMBLE, I did not understand how to keep it in R as you were trying to suggest).

Here is the code:

makeRfuns <- function(keepInR){

  # get samples
  X1 <- keepInR$X1
  X2 <- keepInR$X2
  X3 <- keepInR$X3

  # I can use X1,X2,X3 in all functions here
  # generic function, can be used for both logmu and logphi
  calc_log <- function(c0,c1,c2,c3){
    return(c0 + c1 * X1 + c2 * X2 + c3 * X3)
  }
  return(list(calc_log = calc_log))
}

####### multivariate negative binomial distribution
# density
dNBVector <- nimbleFunction(
  run = function(x      = double(1),
                 logmu  = double(1),
                 logphi = double(1),
                 log    = integer(0, default = 0)) { ## default should be zero
    returnType(double(0))
    # compute p,r out of logmu and logphi
    r       = exp(logphi)
    p       = r/(exp(logmu)+r)
    logProb = sum(dnbinom(x,r,p,log=TRUE))
    if(log) return(logProb) else return(exp(logProb))
  }
)
# random number generation
rNBVector<-nimbleFunction(
  run = function(n      = integer(0),
                 logmu  = double(1),
                 logphi = double(1)) { ## default should be zero
    returnType(double(1))
    # compute p,r out of logmu and logphi
    r  = exp(logphi)
    p  = r/(exp(logmu)+r)
    return(rnbinom(n,r,p))
  }
)

##### obtain Y,X1,X2,X3 somehow

# create a function that computes logmu/logphi
keepInR <- list(X1=X1,X2=X2,X3=X3)

# obtain pointer to calc_log function
Rfuns             <- makeRfuns(keepInR)
calc_log_internal <- Rfuns$calc_log

# now need to register with NIMBLE
calc_log <- nimbleRcall(function(c0=double(0),c1=double(0),c2=double(0),c3=double(0)){},
                        returnType = double(1),
                        Rfun = "calc_log_internal"
                       )

#### create nimble model

modelCode <- nimbleCode({
  #### DP
  # for mean
  for(i in 1:(H-1)){
    v[i] ~ dbeta(1, alpha)
  }
  w[1:H] <- stick_breaking(v[1:(H-1)])

  #for phi
  for(i in 1:(HH-1)){
    vv[i] ~ dbeta(1, alpha2)
  }
  ww[1:HH] <- stick_breaking(vv[1:(HH-1)])

  ### sample from G0
  # mean
  for(h in 1:H){
    a0[h] ~ dnorm(0.0,1.5)

    a1[h] ~ dnorm(0.0,1.5)
    a2[h] ~ dnorm(0.0,1.5)
    a3[h] ~ dnorm(0.0,1.5)

  }
  # phi
  for(hh in 1:HH){
    b0[hh] ~ dnorm(0.0,1.5)

    b1[hh] ~ dnorm(0.0,1.5)
    b2[hh] ~ dnorm(0.0,1.5)
    b3[hh] ~ dnorm(0.0,1.5)

  }

  for(g in 1:G){
    # sample category: zeta[g] in [1......H], and zeta2[g] in [1...HH]
    zeta[g] ~ dcat(w[1:H])
    zeta2[g] ~ dcat(ww[1:HH])

    # try to use our function
    logmu[g,1:T]  <- calc_log(a0[zeta[g]],a1[zeta[g]],a2[zeta[g]],a3[zeta[g]])
    logphi[g,1:T] <- calc_log(b0[zeta2[g]],b1[zeta2[g]],b2[zeta2[g]],b3[zeta2[g]])

    # likelihood
    Y[g,1:T] ~ dNBVector(logmu[g,1:T],logphi[g,1:T])

  }
})

Basically, I did not understand how to return dummy values (either deterministic or stochastic) and keep all the data (Y,X1,X2...) inside a particular scope (I think this is what you meant, but I can be wrong).

Evgenii

messages.body_plain:
Hi Evgeny,

I am really interested to see this application too!

Right, your model is a nonparametric model with a stick-breaking representation for the random measures. Using the CRP representation might be more efficient (well this depends on what values you are using for H and HH and how many cluster are determine by the CRP distribution). I think is worth trying it (see code below).

The functionality for using the CRP in a model such as yours is not yet in our released version (but should be in a month or so) but  you can install the nimble version from devel to use the CRP for your model doing this:

Sys.setenv(R_REMOTES_NO_ERRORS_FROM_WARNINGS="true")
remotes::install_github('nimble-dev/nimble','devel', 'packages/nimble')

If you use the CRP representation you can define H1 < G and HH1 < G cluster parameters (a0, a1, a2, a3, a4, and b0, b1, b2, b3, b4) to reduce compilation time. This will create a warning in the “buildMCMC” step and if ever the sampler needs more cluster parameters than the ones you have available, the sampler will warn you and you should increase the values of H1 and HH1. Also, the CRP has the advantage that only cluster parameters that are occupied are updated so this reduces the run time of the MCMC (again, how much it reduces depends on how many clusters are created).

Under this representation the random measures are integrated out so you don’t get posterior samples of them directly from the MCMC’s output but you can use the getSamplesDPmeasure function which will provide posterior samples of the random measures.

One more thing, if you use the CRP representation and consider gamma prior distributions for the concentration parameters NIMBLE will assign specialized samplers for them. Recall that this parameter affects the number of clusters that are created.

I hope this comments together with Perry’s and Daniel’s inputs are helpful.

Please, let me know if you have any questions or something is not clear enough.

----------------------------------------------------------
Here is how your code would look like:

modelCodeCRP <- nimbleCode({
  # if you want to place prior distributions for the concentration parameter:
  alpha ~ dgamma(c1, d1)
  alpha2 ~ dgamma(c2, d2)

  for(h in 1:H1){ # H1 can be smaller or equal to G

    a0[h] ~ dnorm(0.0,1.5)
    a1[h] ~ ddexp(0.0,1.5)
    a2[h] ~ ddexp(0.0,1.5)
    a3[h] ~ ddexp(0.0,1.5)
    a4[h] ~ ddexp(0.0,1.5)
  }

  for(hh in 1:HH1){ # HH1 can be smaller or equal to G

    b0[hh] ~ dnorm(0.0,1.5)
    b1[hh] ~ ddexp(0.0,1.5)
    b2[hh] ~ ddexp(0.0,1.5)
    b3[hh] ~ ddexp(0.0,1.5)
    b4[hh] ~ ddexp(0.0,1.5)
  }

  zeta[1:G] ~ dCRP(conc = alpha, size = G)
  zeta2[1:G] ~ dCRP(conc = alpha2, size = G)

  # likelihood
  for(g in 1:G){

    for(t in 1:T0){

      Y[g,t] ~ dnegbin(p[g,t],phi[g,t])

      p[g,t]   <- phi[g,t]/(scale_factors[t]*exp(logmu[g,t])+phi[g,t])
      phi[g,t] <- exp(logphi[g,t])

      logmu[g,t] <- a0[zeta[g]] + a1[zeta[g]] * X1[t]+ a2[zeta[g]] * X2[t] + a3[zeta[g]]* X3[t]+ a4[zeta[g]]* X4[t]

      logphi[g,t] <- b0[zeta2[g]] + b1[zeta2[g]] * X1[t] + b2[zeta2[g]] * X2[t] + b3[zeta2[g]] * X3[t] + b4[zeta2[g]] * X4[t]
    }
  }
})

Best,
Claudia

> > > > I'm not an expert on the BNP facilities offered in NIMBLE, but I think I can comment: the stick-breaking representation (as you're using), and the CRP distribution, are modelling the same Dirichlet process.  They differ in the MCMC sampling algorithms which are applied to each, automatically, by NIMBLE's MCMC.  Translating your code between these two (mathematically identical) representations is a relatively small and straight-forward exercise.  The relative performance of the different sampling algorithms, as applied to each representation, could differ, would depend on the model and the data, and is generally difficult to predict.
> > > >
> > > > Changing between the stick-breaking representation and the CRP representation, the categorical distribution would persist in your model.  And Perry's comments are correct, that (in particular for a large number of categories, e.g. large values of H or HH in your code) the categorical sampler (which is applied to the categorical distribution) would become arbitrarily inefficient, in that it evaluates the posterior density for every category value (H or HH times), then samples directly from that posterior distribution.  And that you could hopefully reduce this inefficiency by writing a customized sampling strategy (a custom-written MCMC sampler), to update your categorical distributions, in a more efficient (less wasteful) manner.

> > > > > >

> > > > > >
> > > > > > Going further, you could store logmu itself outside the model, using another dummy variable to serve as a low-dimensional node to establish the graph relationships in the model.  This would look something like

> > > > > >

On Thursday, July 16, 2020 at 6:14:16 AM UTC+1, Claudia Wehrhahn Cortes wrote:

> Hi Evgeny,
>
> I am really interested to see this application too!
>
> Right, your model is a nonparametric model with a stick-breaking representation for the random measures. Using the CRP representation might be more efficient (well this depends on what values you are using for H and HH and how many cluster are determine by the CRP distribution). I think is worth trying it (see code below).
>
> The functionality for using the CRP in a model such as yours is not yet in our released version (but should be in a month or so) but  you can install the nimble version from devel to use the CRP for your model doing this:
>
> Sys.setenv(R_REMOTES_NO_ERRORS_FROM_WARNINGS="true")
> remotes::install_github('nimble-dev/nimble','devel', 'packages/nimble')
>
> If you use the CRP representation you can define H1 < G and HH1 < G cluster parameters (a0, a1, a2, a3, a4, and b0, b1, b2, b3, b4) to reduce compilation time. This will create a warning in the “buildMCMC” step and if ever the sampler needs more cluster parameters than the ones you have available, the sampler will warn you and you should increase the values of H1 and HH1. Also, the CRP has the advantage that only cluster parameters that are occupied are updated so this reduces the run time of the MCMC (again, how much it reduces depends on how many clusters are created).
>
> Under this representation the random measures are integrated out so you don’t get posterior samples of them directly from the MCMC’s output but you can use the getSamplesDPmeasure function which will provide posterior samples of the random measures.
>
> One more thing, if you use the CRP representation and consider gamma prior distributions for the concentration parameters NIMBLE will assign specialized samplers for them. Recall that this parameter affects the number of clusters that are created.
>
> I hope this comments together with Perry’s and Daniel’s inputs are helpful.
>
> Please, let me know if you have any questions or something is not clear enough.
>
> ----------------------------------------------------------
> Here is how your code would look like:
>
> modelCodeCRP <- nimbleCode({
>   # if you want to place prior distributions for the concentration parameter:
>   alpha ~ dgamma(c1, d1)
>   alpha2 ~ dgamma(c2, d2)
>
>   for(h in 1:H1){ # H1 can be smaller or equal to G
>     a0[h] ~ dnorm(0.0,1.5)
>     a1[h] ~ ddexp(0.0,1.5)
>     a2[h] ~ ddexp(0.0,1.5)
>     a3[h] ~ ddexp(0.0,1.5)
>     a4[h] ~ ddexp(0.0,1.5)
>   }
>   for(hh in 1:HH1){ # HH1 can be smaller or equal to G
>     b0[hh] ~ dnorm(0.0,1.5)
>     b1[hh] ~ ddexp(0.0,1.5)
>     b2[hh] ~ ddexp(0.0,1.5)
>     b3[hh] ~ ddexp(0.0,1.5)
>     b4[hh] ~ ddexp(0.0,1.5)
>   }
>
>   zeta[1:G] ~ dCRP(conc = alpha, size = G)
>   zeta2[1:G] ~ dCRP(conc = alpha2, size = G)
>
>   # likelihood
>   for(g in 1:G){
>
>     for(t in 1:T0){
>       Y[g,t] ~ dnegbin(p[g,t],phi[g,t])
>
>       p[g,t]   <- phi[g,t]/(scale_factors[t]*exp(logmu[g,t])+phi[g,t])
>       phi[g,t] <- exp(logphi[g,t])
>
>       logmu[g,t] <- a0[zeta[g]] + a1[zeta[g]] * X1[t]+ a2[zeta[g]] * X2[t] + a3[zeta[g]]* X3[t]+ a4[zeta[g]]* X4[t]
>
>       logphi[g,t] <- b0[zeta2[g]] + b1[zeta2[g]] * X1[t] + b2[zeta2[g]] * X2[t] + b3[zeta2[g]] * X3[t] + b4[zeta2[g]] * X4[t]
>     }
>   }
> })
>
>
> Best,
> Claudia
>

> > > But, if you do decide to look into it, then I'd suggest first reading section15.5 of the NIMBLE user's manual ("Example: writing user-defined samplers to extend NIMBLE’s MCMC engine")
> > > https://r-nimble.org/html_manual/cha-progr-with-models.html#sec:user-samplers
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > On Wed, Jul 15, 2020 at 2:00 PM Evgeny Lobzaev <evgeny...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > I see.
> > > > Well, to be honest, I have no idea how to write such a customized sampler? Like where do I start if I have never done it before?
> > > >
> > > > Evgenii
> > > >
> > > > On Wednesday, July 15, 2020 at 9:45:35 PM UTC+1, Daniel Turek wrote:
> > > > > I'm not an expert on the BNP facilities offered in NIMBLE, but I think I can comment: the stick-breaking representation (as you're using), and the CRP distribution, are modelling the same Dirichlet process.  They differ in the MCMC sampling algorithms which are applied to each, automatically, by NIMBLE's MCMC.  Translating your code between these two (mathematically identical) representations is a relatively small and straight-forward exercise.  The relative performance of the different sampling algorithms, as applied to each representation, could differ, would depend on the model and the data, and is generally difficult to predict.
> > > > >
> > > > > Changing between the stick-breaking representation and the CRP representation, the categorical distribution would persist in your model.  And Perry's comments are correct, that (in particular for a large number of categories, e.g. large values of H or HH in your code) the categorical sampler (which is applied to the categorical distribution) would become arbitrarily inefficient, in that it evaluates the posterior density for every category value (H or HH times), then samples directly from that posterior distribution.  And that you could hopefully reduce this inefficiency by writing a customized sampling strategy (a custom-written MCMC sampler), to update your categorical distributions, in a more efficient (less wasteful) manner.
> > > > >
> > > > > Hope this helps,
> > > > > Daniel
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >

> > > > > >
> > > > > > Evgenii
> > > > > >

> > > > > > On Wednesday, July 15, 2020 at 3:41:48 PM UTC+1, pdevalpine wrote:

> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > I commented on why nimble encounters memory problems (which we hope to improve).  Then I gave a strategy for keeping large objects out of the model.  That strategy might work well for your problem.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Looking at your model, I wonder if the following would work: Vectorize logmu and logphi over t (since any change in a parameter will affect all t).  And use a vector of dummy data values to push calculation of phi[g, 1:T], p[g, 1:T] and log probabilities of y[g, 1:T] to R (or C++) using the trick I showed in the June 26 message.  Your model code would have something like:
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > dummy[g] ~ dCustom(logmu[g, 1:T],  logphi[g, 1:T], g ) # do the phi, p and y steps all together
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > All the actual values of y would live in dCustom.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > This could also be done for logmu and/or logphi at a couple of levels.  You could have
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > logmu[g, 1:T] <- calc_logmu(a0[zeta[g]], a1[zeta[g]], etc.)
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > All of the values of X would live in calc_logmu.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Going further, you could store logmu itself outside the model, using another dummy variable to serve as a low-dimensional node to establish the graph relationships in the model.  This would look something like
> > > > > > >

> > > > > > >

> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > This is all something of a workaround to the scaling issues, but it is fairly straightforward to set up once you see how the pieces fit together and allows nimble to manage the model graph and MCMC system.   I'm happy to help sort it out if it's not clear how it all can fit together.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > A couple of final thoughts on your model: Sampling for dcat can be inefficient because on every iteration every possible value is tried. Hi Evgeny,

R CMD build nimble

to install nimble.

-chris

On Thu, Jul 16, 2020 at 2:58 AM Evgeny Lobzaev <evgeny....@gmail.com> wrote:

> Hi Claudia,
>
> Thank you for your response. I may be doing something wrong but I am receiving the following error:
> sampler_CRP: At the moment, NIMBLE can only sample when there is one variable being clustered for each cluster membershipID. When I use non-vectorized code (i.e. as the one in your snippet).
> sampler_CRP: CRP_nonconjugate sampler not yet set up to handle clustering of more than three variables. When I use vectorized form (i.e. as the one which I posted in one of the messages above).

> Evgenii

> On Thursday, July 16, 2020 at 6:14:16 AM UTC+1, Claudia Wehrhahn Cortes wrote:
> > Hi Evgeny,
> >
> > I am really interested to see this application too!
> >
> > Right, your model is a nonparametric model with a stick-breaking representation for the random measures. Using the CRP representation might be more efficient (well this depends on what values you are using for H and HH and how many cluster are determine by the CRP distribution). I think is worth trying it (see code below).
> >
> > The functionality for using the CRP in a model such as yours is not yet in our released version (but should be in a month or so) but  you can install the nimble version from devel to use the CRP for your model doing this:
> >
> > Sys.setenv(R_REMOTES_NO_ERRORS_FROM_WARNINGS="true")
> > remotes::install_github('nimble-dev/nimble','devel', 'packages/nimble')
> >
> > If you use the CRP representation you can define H1 < G and HH1 < G cluster parameters (a0, a1, a2, a3, a4, and b0, b1, b2, b3, b4) to reduce compilation time. This will create a warning in the “buildMCMC” step and if ever the sampler needs more cluster parameters than the ones you have available, the sampler will warn you and you should increase the values of H1 and HH1. Also, the CRP has the advantage that only cluster parameters that are occupied are updated so this reduces the run time of the MCMC (again, how much it reduces depends on how many clusters are created).
> >
> > Under this representation the random measures are integrated out so you don’t get posterior samples of them directly from the MCMC’s output but you can use the getSamplesDPmeasure function which will provide posterior samples of the random measures.
> >
> > One more thing, if you use the CRP representation and consider gamma prior distributions for the concentration parameters NIMBLE will assign specialized samplers for them. Recall that this parameter affects the number of clusters that are created.
> >
> > I hope this comments together with Perry’s and Daniel’s inputs are helpful.
> >
> > Please, let me know if you have any questions or something is not clear enough.
> >
> > ----------------------------------------------------------
> > Here is how your code would look like:
> >
> > modelCodeCRP <- nimbleCode({
> >   # if you want to place prior distributions for the concentration parameter:
> >   alpha ~ dgamma(c1, d1)
> >   alpha2 ~ dgamma(c2, d2)
> >
> >   for(h in 1:H1){ # H1 can be smaller or equal to G
> >     a0[h] ~ dnorm(0.0,1.5)
> >     a1[h] ~ ddexp(0.0,1.5)
> >     a2[h] ~ ddexp(0.0,1.5)
> >     a3[h] ~ ddexp(0.0,1.5)
> >     a4[h] ~ ddexp(0.0,1.5)
> >   }
> >   for(hh in 1:HH1){ # HH1 can be smaller or equal to G
> >     b0[hh] ~ dnorm(0.0,1.5)
> >     b1[hh] ~ ddexp(0.0,1.5)
> >     b2[hh] ~ ddexp(0.0,1.5)
> >     b3[hh] ~ ddexp(0.0,1.5)
> >     b4[hh] ~ ddexp(0.0,1.5)
> >   }
> >
> >   zeta[1:G] ~ dCRP(conc = alpha, size = G)
> >   zeta2[1:G] ~ dCRP(conc = alpha2, size = G)
> >
> >   # likelihood
> >   for(g in 1:G){
> >
> >     for(t in 1:T0){
> >       Y[g,t] ~ dnegbin(p[g,t],phi[g,t])
> >
> >       p[g,t]   <- phi[g,t]/(scale_factors[t]*exp(logmu[g,t])+phi[g,t])
> >       phi[g,t] <- exp(logphi[g,t])
> >
> >       logmu[g,t] <- a0[zeta[g]] + a1[zeta[g]] * X1[t]+ a2[zeta[g]] * X2[t] + a3[zeta[g]]* X3[t]+ a4[zeta[g]]* X4[t]
> >
> >       logphi[g,t] <- b0[zeta2[g]] + b1[zeta2[g]] * X1[t] + b2[zeta2[g]] * X2[t] + b3[zeta2[g]] * X3[t] + b4[zeta2[g]] * X4[t]
> >     }
> >   }
> > })
> >
> >
> > Best,
> > Claudia
> >
> > On Wed, Jul 15, 2020 at 3:28 PM Evgeny Lobzaev <evgeny...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > Ok, need to take a look at that chapter! Thank you, Daniel.
> > >
> > > Perry,
> > >
> > > I am not sure I managed to incorporate all your ideas in the code (as I did not fully understand all of the points). However, I did the following and it seemed to improve the speed. I am still wondering if additional improvement can be achieved (particularly, I am still sending count data matrix Y to NIMBLE, I did not understand how to keep it in R as you were trying to suggest).
> > >
> > > Here is the code:
> > >
> > >
> > > makeRfuns <- function(keepInR){
> > >
> > >   # get samples
> > >   X1 <- keepInR$X1
> > >   X2 <- keepInR$X2
> > >   X3 <- keepInR$X3

> > >   # I can use X1,X2,X3 in all functions here
> > >   # generic function, can be used for both logmu and logphi
> > >   calc_log <- function(c0,c1,c2,c3){

> > >   }

> > >
> > > ####### multivariate negative binomial distribution

> > > dNBVector <- nimbleFunction(
> > >   run = function(x      = double(1),
> > >                  logmu  = double(1),
> > >                  logphi = double(1),

> > >   }
> > > )
> > > # random number generation
> > > rNBVector<-nimbleFunction(
> > >   run = function(n      = integer(0),
> > >                  logmu  = double(1),
> > >                  logphi = double(1)) { ## default should be zero
> > >     returnType(double(1))
> > >     # compute p,r out of logmu and logphi
> > >     r  = exp(logphi)
> > >     p  = r/(exp(logmu)+r)
> > >     return(rnbinom(n,r,p))
> > >   }
> > > )
> > >
> > > ##### obtain Y,X1,X2,X3 somehow
> > >
> > > # create a function that computes logmu/logphi
> > > keepInR <- list(X1=X1,X2=X2,X3=X3)
> > >
> > > # obtain pointer to calc_log function
> > > Rfuns             <- makeRfuns(keepInR)
> > > calc_log_internal <- Rfuns$calc_log
> > >
> > > # now need to register with NIMBLE
> > > calc_log <- nimbleRcall(function(c0=double(0),c1=double(0),c2=double(0),c3=double(0)){},
> > >                         returnType = double(1),
> > >                         Rfun = "calc_log_internal"
> > >                        )
> > >
> > > #### create nimble model
> > > modelCode <- nimbleCode({
> > >   #### DP
> > >   # for mean
> > >   for(i in 1:(H-1)){
> > >     v[i] ~ dbeta(1, alpha)
> > >   }
> > >   w[1:H] <- stick_breaking(v[1:(H-1)])
> > >
> > >   #for phi
> > >   for(i in 1:(HH-1)){
> > >     vv[i] ~ dbeta(1, alpha2)
> > >   }
> > >   ww[1:HH] <- stick_breaking(vv[1:(HH-1)])
> > >
> > >   ### sample from G0
> > >   # mean
> > >   for(h in 1:H){
> > >     a0[h] ~ dnorm(0.0,1.5)
> > >     a1[h] ~ dnorm(0.0,1.5)
> > >     a2[h] ~ dnorm(0.0,1.5)
> > >     a3[h] ~ dnorm(0.0,1.5)
> > >   }
> > >   # phi
> > >   for(hh in 1:HH){
> > >     b0[hh] ~ dnorm(0.0,1.5)
> > >     b1[hh] ~ dnorm(0.0,1.5)
> > >     b2[hh] ~ dnorm(0.0,1.5)
> > >     b3[hh] ~ dnorm(0.0,1.5)
> > >   }
> > >
> > >   for(g in 1:G){
> > >     # sample category: zeta[g] in [1......H], and zeta2[g] in [1...HH]
> > >     zeta[g] ~ dcat(w[1:H])
> > >     zeta2[g] ~ dcat(ww[1:HH])
> > >
> > >     # try to use our function
> > >     logmu[g,1:T]  <- calc_log(a0[zeta[g]],a1[zeta[g]],a2[zeta[g]],a3[zeta[g]])
> > >     logphi[g,1:T] <- calc_log(b0[zeta2[g]],b1[zeta2[g]],b2[zeta2[g]],b3[zeta2[g]])
> > >
> > >     # likelihood
> > >     Y[g,1:T] ~ dNBVector(logmu[g,1:T],logphi[g,1:T])
> > >
> > >   }
> > > })
> > >
> > > Basically, I did not understand how to return dummy values (either deterministic or stochastic) and keep all the data (Y,X1,X2...) inside a particular scope (I think this is what you meant, but I can be wrong).
> > >
> > > Evgenii
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > On Wednesday, July 15, 2020 at 10:27:54 PM UTC+1, Daniel Turek wrote:
> > > > You may or may not need to go down the road of writing a customized sampler for your model.  It really depends on your model, whether this is worthwhile.  I would see how performance (speed and mixing) of the MCMC is sampling is, before starting with that.
> > > >
> > > > But, if you do decide to look into it, then I'd suggest first reading section15.5 of the NIMBLE user's manual ("Example: writing user-defined samplers to extend NIMBLE’s MCMC engine")
> > > > https://r-nimble.org/html_manual/cha-progr-with-models.html#sec:user-samplers
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > On Wed, Jul 15, 2020 at 2:00 PM Evgeny Lobzaev <evgeny...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > I see.
> > > > > Well, to be honest, I have no idea how to write such a customized sampler? Like where do I start if I have never done it before?
> > > > >
> > > > > Evgenii
> > > > >
> > > > > On Wednesday, July 15, 2020 at 9:45:35 PM UTC+1, Daniel Turek wrote:
> > > > > > I'm not an expert on the BNP facilities offered in NIMBLE, but I think I can comment: the stick-breaking representation (as you're using), and the CRP distribution, are modelling the same Dirichlet process.  They differ in the MCMC sampling algorithms which are applied to each, automatically, by NIMBLE's MCMC.  Translating your code between these two (mathematically identical) representations is a relatively small and straight-forward exercise.  The relative performance of the different sampling algorithms, as applied to each representation, could differ, would depend on the model and the data, and is generally difficult to predict.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Changing between the stick-breaking representation and the CRP representation, the categorical distribution would persist in your model.  And Perry's comments are correct, that (in particular for a large number of categories, e.g. large values of H or HH in your code) the categorical sampler (which is applied to the categorical distribution) would become arbitrarily inefficient, in that it evaluates the posterior density for every category value (H or HH times), then samples directly from that posterior distribution.  And that you could hopefully reduce this inefficiency by writing a customized sampling strategy (a custom-written MCMC sampler), to update your categorical distributions, in a more efficient (less wasteful) manner.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Hope this helps,
> > > > > > Daniel
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > On Wed, Jul 15, 2020 at 8:19 AM Evgeny Lobzaev <evgeny...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > > > Hi Perry!

> > > > > > >

But this is essentially what I am using right now: I just took a stick-breaking DP representation from chapter 10.3.2 in the documentation. In that example categorical distribution is used. Are you suggesting to replace the stick-breaking representation with the CRP (to avoid using categorical distribution)? Or did you mean something else?
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Evgenii
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > On Wednesday, July 15, 2020 at 3:41:48 PM UTC+1, pdevalpine wrote:
> > > > > > > > Hi Evgeny,
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > Thanks for the message and I'm very interested to see this application.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > Let me point you to my message of June 26 on this thread:
> > > > > > > > https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/nimble-users/8vaTHQoJz2M
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > I commented on why nimble encounters memory problems (which we hope to improve).  Then I gave a strategy for keeping large objects out of the model.  That strategy might work well for your problem.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > Looking at your model, I wonder if the following would work: Vectorize logmu and logphi over t (since any change in a parameter will affect all t).  And use a vector of dummy data values to push calculation of phi[g, 1:T], p[g, 1:T] and log probabilities of y[g, 1:T] to R (or C++) using the trick I showed in the June 26 message.  Your model code would have something like:
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > dummy[g] ~ dCustom(logmu[g, 1:T],  logphi[g, 1:T], g ) # do the phi, p and y steps all together
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > All the actual values of y would live in dCustom.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > This could also be done for logmu and/or logphi at a couple of levels.  You could have
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > logmu[g, 1:T] <- calc_logmu(a0[zeta[g]], a1[zeta[g]], etc.)
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > All of the values of X would live in calc_logmu.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > Going further, you could store logmu itself outside the model, using another dummy variable to serve as a low-dimensional node to establish the graph relationships in the model.  This would look something like
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > logmu_dummy[g] <- calc_logmu(g, a0[zeta[g]], a1[zeta[g]], etc.)
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > where calc_logmu would have to return a value to logmu_dummy[g] that wouldn't really matter.  The actual values of logmu would be stored in R (or C++) in the same scope from where they'd be used by dCustom.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > This is all something of a workaround to the scaling issues, but it is fairly straightforward to set up once you see how the pieces fit together and allows nimble to manage the model graph and MCMC system.   I'm happy to help sort it out if it's not clear how it all can fit together.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > A couple of final thoughts on your model: Sampling for dcat can be inefficient because on every iteration every possible value is tried.  It would be easy to set up a sampler that for example tries one alternative or a random subset of alternatives.  Computational cost vs. mixing is hard to predict and would depend on the model.  The dcat case is a tradeoff I've been curious about. Also, you may be good with what you've written, but nimble does have Bayesian non-parametric distributions (see blog posts linked from our documentation page at r-nimble.org <http://r-nimble.org>) and they will be improved in an upcoming release.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > HTH and let me know how it goes.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > -Perry

I just tried this model with 'dcar_proper' (along with its respective changes to the parameters), and I'm having the same issue. Model is defined, but 'configureMCMC' runs for about 4 minutes and then R crashes.

On Wednesday, July 15, 2020 at 11:10:49 PM UTC-6 Liz Lawler wrote:
> Oh, also! This is the first model I've used 'dcar_normal' in, so I'm not sure if that could be the issue. I've used 'dcar_proper' in the past with no issues.
>
> On Wednesday, July 15, 2020 at 10:53:08 PM UTC-6 Liz Lawler wrote:
> > Hi!
> >
> > I'm hoping you might be able to help me figure out why configureMCMC crashes after a few minutes (and why it's taking so long in the first place!). The code I'm executing is below. Happy to share the data if you'd like to fully replicate this.
> >
> > I've tried this on both my local machine and rstudio server on google cloud. Everything runs well through the 'ZIPmod' line; 'configureMCMC' is where my issues appear. My local machine continually runs and freezes, whereas rstudio server will run for a few minutes and then crash. I haven't had issues with this in the past on different models, so I'm wondering if it's something in this model that's holding things up.
> >
> > Thank you in advance for any help/advice you might be able to provide me - I really appreciate it!
> >
> >
> > library(nimble)
> > library(coda)
> > library(MASS)
> >
> > dZIP <- nimbleFunction(
> >   run = function(x = integer(), lambda = double(), zeroProb = double(),
> >                  log = logical(0, default = 0)) {
> >     returnType(double())
> >     if (x != 0) {
> >       if (log) return(dpois(x, lambda, log = TRUE) + log(1- zeroProb))
> >       else return((1 - zeroProb) * dpois(x, lambda, log = FALSE))
> >     }
> >     totalProbZero <- zeroProb + (1 - zeroProb) * dpois(0, lambda, log = FALSE)
> >     if (log) return(log(totalProbZero))
> >     return(totalProbZero)
> >   }
> > )
> >
> >
> > full_X <- X_30_eq_tc
> > full_y <- train_counts$n_fire
> >
> > # subset to test if model works
> > # do t = 4 to start -> 336 observations (84 spatial regions * 4 timesteps)
> > X_sub <- full_X[1:336,]
> > y_sub <- full_y[1:336]
> >
> > log_area = log(area_df$area * 1e-11) / 2
> >
> > s <- 84

messages.subject_clean: configureMCMC too slow and eventually crashes R
messages.body_plain:
Hi Liz,

Thanks for the question.

It's probably the long chain of deterministic dependencies.  The system for determining conjugate relationships among stochastic nodes gets clogged up tracing through those.  It's clearly something that needs improvement.  The workaround (I hope!) is to do useConjugacy=FALSE in configureMCMC.

If there is any way you can rewrite the temporal part of the model to avoid the long chains of dependencies, you might get better performance anyway.  Sometimes it is possible to rearrange what is stochastic and what is deterministic in a way that reduces the chain of calculations needed for MCMC updates.  You may be well aware of this, and I haven't looked at your model carefully enough to see if this looks feasible, but I'm just mentioning it as a general comment.

-Perry

> > > >
> > > > The functionality for using the CRP in a model such as yours is not yet in our released version (but should be in a month or so) but  you can install the nimble version from devel to use the CRP for your model doing this:

> > > > remotes::install_github('nimble-dev/nimble','devel', 'packages/nimble')

> > > > If you use the CRP representation you can define H1 < G and HH1 < G cluster parameters (a0, a1, a2, a3, a4, and b0, b1, b2, b3, b4) to reduce compilation time. Also, the CRP has the advantage that only cluster parameters that are occupied are updated so this reduces the run time of the MCMC (again, how much it reduces depends on how many clusters are created).
> > > >
> > > > Under this representation the random measures are integrated out so you don’t get posterior samples of them directly from the MCMC’s output but you can use the getSamplesDPmeasure function which will provide posterior samples of the random measures.
> > > >
> > > > One more thing, if you use the CRP representation and consider gamma prior distributions for the concentration parameters NIMBLE will assign specialized samplers for them. Recall that this parameter affects the number of clusters that are created.
> > > >

> > > >     b4[hh] ~ ddexp(0.0,1.5)

> > > >   # likelihood

> > > > > > > > I'm not an expert on the BNP facilities offered in NIMBLE, but I think I can comment: the stick-breaking representation (as you're using), and the CRP distribution, are modelling the same Dirichlet process.  They differ in the MCMC sampling algorithms which are applied to each, automatically, by NIMBLE's MCMC.  Translating your code between these two (mathematically identical) representations is a relatively small and straight-forward exercise.  The relative performance of the different sampling algorithms, as applied to each representation, could differ, would depend on the model and the data, and is generally difficult to predict.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > Changing between the stick-breaking representation and the CRP representation, the categorical distribution would persist in your model.  And Perry's comments are correct, that (in particular for a large number of categories, e.g. large values of H or HH in your code) the categorical sampler (which is applied to the categorical distribution) would become arbitrarily inefficient, in that it evaluates the posterior density for every category value (H or HH times), then samples directly from that posterior distribution.  And that you could hopefully reduce this inefficiency by writing a customized sampling strategy (a custom-written MCMC sampler), to update your categorical distributions, in a more efficient (less wasteful) manner.

> > > > > > > > > > A couple of final thoughts on your model: Sampling for dcat can be inefficient because on every iteration every possible value is tried.  It would be easy to set up a sampler that for example tries one alternative or a random subset of alternatives.  Computational cost vs. mixing is hard to predict and would depend on the model.  The dcat case is a tradeoff I've been curious about. Also, you may be good with what you've written, but nimble does have Bayesian non-parametric distributions (see blog posts linked from our documentation page at r-nimble.org <http://r-nimble.org>) and they will be improved in an upcoming release.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Perry,

That did the trick - thank you so much! It worked instantaneously.

Are there downsides to setting useConjugacy = FALSE? In the future, would you suggest I only use this if I have extreme slowdown issues like the above?

best,
Liz

On Thursday, July 16, 2020 at 11:47:30 AM UTC-6 pdevalpine wrote:
> Hi Liz,
>
> Thanks for the question.
>
> It's probably the long chain of deterministic dependencies.  The system for determining conjugate relationships among stochastic nodes gets clogged up tracing through those.  It's clearly something that needs improvement.  The workaround (I hope!) is to do useConjugacy=FALSE in configureMCMC.
>
> If there is any way you can rewrite the temporal part of the model to avoid the long chains of dependencies, you might get better performance anyway.  Sometimes it is possible to rearrange what is stochastic and what is deterministic in a way that reduces the chain of calculations needed for MCMC updates.  You may be well aware of this, and I haven't looked at your model carefully enough to see if this looks feasible, but I'm just mentioning it as a general comment.
>
> -Perry
>

> > > > sampler_CRP: CRP_nonconjugate sampler not yet set up to handle clustering of more than three variables. When I use vectorized form (i.e. as the one which I posted in one of the messages above).

> > > > > Hi Evgeny,
> > > > >
> > > > > I am really interested to see this application too!
> > > > >
> > > > > Right, your model is a nonparametric model with a stick-breaking representation for the random measures. Using the CRP representation might be more efficient (well this depends on what values you are using for H and HH and how many cluster are determine by the CRP distribution). I think is worth trying it (see code below).
> > > > >
> > > > > The functionality for using the CRP in a model such as yours is not yet in our released version (but should be in a month or so) but  you can install the nimble version from devel to use the CRP for your model doing this:
> > > > >
> > > > > Sys.setenv(R_REMOTES_NO_ERRORS_FROM_WARNINGS="true")
> > > > > remotes::install_github('nimble-dev/nimble','devel', 'packages/nimble')
> > > > >
> > > > > If you use the CRP representation you can define H1 < G and HH1 < G cluster parameters (a0, a1, a2, a3, a4, and b0, b1, b2, b3, b4) to reduce compilation time. This will create a warning in the “buildMCMC” step and if ever the sampler needs more cluster parameters than the ones you have available, the sampler will warn you and you should increase the values of H1 and HH1. Also, the CRP has the advantage that only cluster parameters that are occupied are updated so this reduces the run time of the MCMC (again, how much it reduces depends on how many clusters are created).
> > > > >
> > > > > Under this representation the random measures are integrated out so you don’t get posterior samples of them directly from the MCMC’s output but you can use the getSamplesDPmeasure function which will provide posterior samples of the random measures.
> > > > >
> > > > > One more thing, if you use the CRP representation and consider gamma prior distributions for the concentration parameters NIMBLE will assign specialized samplers for them. Recall that this parameter affects the number of clusters that are created.
> > > > >
> > > > > I hope this comments together with Perry’s and Daniel’s inputs are helpful.
> > > > >
> > > > > Please, let me know if you have any questions or something is not clear enough.
> > > > >
> > > > > ----------------------------------------------------------

> > > > >
> > > > > modelCodeCRP <- nimbleCode({
> > > > >   # if you want to place prior distributions for the concentration parameter:
> > > > >   alpha ~ dgamma(c1, d1)
> > > > >   alpha2 ~ dgamma(c2, d2)
> > > > >
> > > > >   for(h in 1:H1){ # H1 can be smaller or equal to G
> > > > >     a0[h] ~ dnorm(0.0,1.5)
> > > > >     a1[h] ~ ddexp(0.0,1.5)
> > > > >     a2[h] ~ ddexp(0.0,1.5)
> > > > >     a3[h] ~ ddexp(0.0,1.5)
> > > > >     a4[h] ~ ddexp(0.0,1.5)
> > > > >   }
> > > > >   for(hh in 1:HH1){ # HH1 can be smaller or equal to G
> > > > >     b0[hh] ~ dnorm(0.0,1.5)
> > > > >     b1[hh] ~ ddexp(0.0,1.5)
> > > > >     b2[hh] ~ ddexp(0.0,1.5)
> > > > >     b3[hh] ~ ddexp(0.0,1.5)
> > > > >     b4[hh] ~ ddexp(0.0,1.5)
> > > > >   }
> > > > >
> > > > >   zeta[1:G] ~ dCRP(conc = alpha, size = G)
> > > > >   zeta2[1:G] ~ dCRP(conc = alpha2, size = G)
> > > > >
> > > > >   # likelihood
> > > > >   for(g in 1:G){
> > > > >
> > > > >     for(t in 1:T0){
> > > > >       Y[g,t] ~ dnegbin(p[g,t],phi[g,t])
> > > > >
> > > > >       p[g,t]   <- phi[g,t]/(scale_factors[t]*exp(logmu[g,t])+phi[g,t])
> > > > >       phi[g,t] <- exp(logphi[g,t])
> > > > >
> > > > >       logmu[g,t] <- a0[zeta[g]] + a1[zeta[g]] * X1[t]+ a2[zeta[g]] * X2[t] + a3[zeta[g]]* X3[t]+ a4[zeta[g]]* X4[t]
> > > > >
> > > > >       logphi[g,t] <- b0[zeta2[g]] + b1[zeta2[g]] * X1[t] + b2[zeta2[g]] * X2[t] + b3[zeta2[g]] * X3[t] + b4[zeta2[g]] * X4[t]
> > > > >     }
> > > > >   }
> > > > > })
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > Best,
> > > > > Claudia

> > > > > > > > On Wednesday, July 15, 2020 at 9:45:35 PM UTC+1, Daniel Turek wrote:
> > > > > > > > > I'm not an expert on the BNP facilities offered in NIMBLE, but I think I can comment: the stick-breaking representation (as you're using), and the CRP distribution, are modelling the same Dirichlet process.  They differ in the MCMC sampling algorithms which are applied to each, automatically, by NIMBLE's MCMC.  Translating your code between these two (mathematically identical) representations is a relatively small and straight-forward exercise.  The relative performance of the different sampling algorithms, as applied to each representation, could differ, would depend on the model and the data, and is generally difficult to predict.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > Changing between the stick-breaking representation and the CRP representation, the categorical distribution would persist in your model.  And Perry's comments are correct, that (in particular for a large number of categories, e.g. large values of H or HH in your code) the categorical sampler (which is applied to the categorical distribution) would become arbitrarily inefficient, in that it evaluates the posterior density for every category value (H or HH times), then samples directly from that posterior distribution.  And that you could hopefully reduce this inefficiency by writing a customized sampling strategy (a custom-written MCMC sampler), to update your categorical distributions, in a more efficient (less wasteful) manner.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > Hope this helps,
> > > > > > > > > Daniel

messages.body_plain:
Hi Evgenii,

Well, this has been a very interesting case on multiple fronts.  Let me respond on the issues of vectorizing and keeping large objects out of the model and in R instead.  It looks like you made a lot of progress on both.  Great to see that you got those pieces working.

Let me explain more about what happens with a stochastic declaration and what I meant about keeping the large Y matrix out of the model.

A stochastic declaration like
Y[g,1:T] ~ dNBVector(logmu[g,1:T],logphi[g,1:T])    #(I am just using the most recent code in front of me.)
tells nimble that Y[g, 1:T] is a (vector, in this case) stochastic node.  This means two things: Y[g, 1:T] will be built into the graph for determining dependencies among nodes.  And the way to calculate the log probability is:
logProb_Y[g, 1] <- dNBVector(Y[g, 1:T], logmu[g,1:T],logphi[g,1:T])

So you could do the following:
proxy_Y[g] ~ dNBVector(logmu[g,1:T],logphi[g,1:T], g)
provide proxy_Y[g] as data to the model.  Its values won't matter.
Now the two things above will be: proxy_Y[g] will be built into the graph, doing the job of Y[g, 1:T.  For example, proxy_Y[g] will be a dependency of logmu[g, 1:T].  And the way to calculate the log probability will be:
logProb_proxy_Y[g] <- dNBVector(proxy_Y[g], logmu[g,1:T], logphi[g,1:T], g)

Then you can create dNBVector as follows:
Add it to the list of functions returned from makeRfuns.
Include Y in the keepInR list so dNBVector can access its values by scoping just as calc_log accesses X1, X2, X3.
Use the same steps as you use for calc_log, i.e. dNBVector_internal and then a nimbleRcall called dNBVector.
Notice that if dNBVector takes g as an argument (as shown above), then it can pick out the correct row of Y to use.
dNBVector must take proxy_Y[g] as its first argument, but it can just ignore it.
Have dNBVector return the log probability of all of Y[g, 1:T].  This will be stored as the log probability of proxy_Y[g].

I hope it makes enough sense to follow!  If I had more time at the moment I would draft it out more fully for you, but let me know if it doesn't work smoothly.

-Perry

>     if(log) return(logProb) else return(exp(logProb))

> )

> rNBVector<-nimbleFunction(
>   run = function(n      = integer(0),
>                  logmu  = double(1),
>                  logphi = double(1)) { ## default should be zero
>     returnType(double(1))

>     return(rnbinom(n,r,p))

> keepInR <- list(X1=X1,X2=X2,X3=X3)
