> Rfuns             <- makeRfuns(keepInR)

> # now need to register with NIMBLE

>                         returnType = double(1),
>                         Rfun = "calc_log_internal"
>                        )

messages.body_plain:
Hi Perry!

Thank you for detailed explanation. I think I understood what needs to be done. I created a code and it works.

I have few concerns/points to mention.
 When I declared a proxy_Y node, I had to make it vector-valued(i.e. proxy_Y[g,1:T] instead of suggested proxy_Y[g]). Otherwise, the c++ compilation fails.
I tested 2 instances of the code: one where I keep matrix Y in R and one where I supply matrix Y to nimble. The second case surprisingly runs a bit faster. Is it because of C++ <-> R  data passing overhead or what can be the reason?
In both versions I had to provide not just a density function for multivariate Negative Binomial distribution (dNBVector) but also a random number generating function (rNBVector). In 2 different situations (provide/not provide Y to nimble) the dNBVector function is coded slightly differently. I wonder if that can contribute to performance issues as well?
In fact, I will share both versions (that is whether or not Y is supplied to nimble) and, if you have some time/desire, you can take a look.
I have to say, this is very kind of you and other team members of NIMBLE to help me. You are really helping me with my project and I appreciate that a lot!

Evgenii

On Thursday, July 16, 2020 at 9:01:58 PM UTC+1, pdevalpine wrote:

> Hi Evgenii,
>
> Well, this has been a very interesting case on multiple fronts.  Let me respond on the issues of vectorizing and keeping large objects out of the model and in R instead.  It looks like you made a lot of progress on both.  Great to see that you got those pieces working.
>
> Let me explain more about what happens with a stochastic declaration and what I meant about keeping the large Y matrix out of the model.
>
> A stochastic declaration like
> Y[g,1:T] ~ dNBVector(logmu[g,1:T],logphi[g,1:T])    #(I am just using the most recent code in front of me.)
> tells nimble that Y[g, 1:T] is a (vector, in this case) stochastic node.  This means two things: Y[g, 1:T] will be built into the graph for determining dependencies among nodes.  And the way to calculate the log probability is:
> logProb_Y[g, 1] <- dNBVector(Y[g, 1:T], logmu[g,1:T],logphi[g,1:T])
>
> So you could do the following:
> proxy_Y[g] ~ dNBVector(logmu[g,1:T],logphi[g,1:T], g)
> provide proxy_Y[g] as data to the model.  Its values won't matter.
> Now the two things above will be: proxy_Y[g] will be built into the graph, doing the job of Y[g, 1:T.  For example, proxy_Y[g] will be a dependency of logmu[g, 1:T].  And the way to calculate the log probability will be:
> logProb_proxy_Y[g] <- dNBVector(proxy_Y[g], logmu[g,1:T], logphi[g,1:T], g)
>
> Then you can create dNBVector as follows:
> Add it to the list of functions returned from makeRfuns.
> Include Y in the keepInR list so dNBVector can access its values by scoping just as calc_log accesses X1, X2, X3.
> Use the same steps as you use for calc_log, i.e. dNBVector_internal and then a nimbleRcall called dNBVector.
> Notice that if dNBVector takes g as an argument (as shown above), then it can pick out the correct row of Y to use.
> dNBVector must take proxy_Y[g] as its first argument, but it can just ignore it.
> Have dNBVector return the log probability of all of Y[g, 1:T].  This will be stored as the log probability of proxy_Y[g].
>
> I hope it makes enough sense to follow!  If I had more time at the moment I would draft it out more fully for you, but let me know if it doesn't work smoothly.
>
> -Perry
>
>
>
>

Hi Evgeny,

a difference between NIMBLE's behavior on R 3.6 and R 4.0 with regard
to
setting up the MCMC sampler for the CRP node, and I suspect you are using R 4.0.

branch, I think it should be fine for you now.

-chris

>> Well, this has been a very interesting case on multiple fronts.  Let me respond on the issues of vectorizing and keeping large objects out of the model and in R instead.  It looks like you made a lot of progress on both.  Great to see that you got those pieces working.
>>
>> Let me explain more about what happens with a stochastic declaration and what I meant about keeping the large Y matrix out of the model.
>>
>> A stochastic declaration like
>> Y[g,1:T] ~ dNBVector(logmu[g,1:T],logphi[g,1:T])    #(I am just using the most recent code in front of me.)
>> tells nimble that Y[g, 1:T] is a (vector, in this case) stochastic node.  This means two things: Y[g, 1:T] will be built into the graph for determining dependencies among nodes.  And the way to calculate the log probability is:
>> logProb_Y[g, 1] <- dNBVector(Y[g, 1:T], logmu[g,1:T],logphi[g,1:T])
>>
>> So you could do the following:
>> proxy_Y[g] ~ dNBVector(logmu[g,1:T],logphi[g,1:T], g)
>> provide proxy_Y[g] as data to the model.  Its values won't matter.
>> Now the two things above will be: proxy_Y[g] will be built into the graph, doing the job of Y[g, 1:T.  For example, proxy_Y[g] will be a dependency of logmu[g, 1:T].  And the way to calculate the log probability will be:
>> logProb_proxy_Y[g] <- dNBVector(proxy_Y[g], logmu[g,1:T], logphi[g,1:T], g)
>>
>> Then you can create dNBVector as follows:
>> Add it to the list of functions returned from makeRfuns.
>> Include Y in the keepInR list so dNBVector can access its values by scoping just as calc_log accesses X1, X2, X3.
>> Use the same steps as you use for calc_log, i.e. dNBVector_internal and then a nimbleRcall called dNBVector.
>> Notice that if dNBVector takes g as an argument (as shown above), then it can pick out the correct row of Y to use.
>> dNBVector must take proxy_Y[g] as its first argument, but it can just ignore it.
>> Have dNBVector return the log probability of all of Y[g, 1:T].  This will be stored as the log probability of proxy_Y[g].
>>
>> I hope it makes enough sense to follow!  If I had more time at the moment I would draft it out more fully for you, but let me know if it doesn't work smoothly.
>>
>> -Perry
>>

> >>
> >> Let me explain more about what happens with a stochastic declaration and what I meant about keeping the large Y matrix out of the model.
> >>
> >> A stochastic declaration like
> >> Y[g,1:T] ~ dNBVector(logmu[g,1:T],logphi[g,1:T])    #(I am just using the most recent code in front of me.)
> >> tells nimble that Y[g, 1:T] is a (vector, in this case) stochastic node.  This means two things: Y[g, 1:T] will be built into the graph for determining dependencies among nodes.  And the way to calculate the log probability is:
> >> logProb_Y[g, 1] <- dNBVector(Y[g, 1:T], logmu[g,1:T],logphi[g,1:T])
> >>
> >> So you could do the following:
> >> proxy_Y[g] ~ dNBVector(logmu[g,1:T],logphi[g,1:T], g)
> >> provide proxy_Y[g] as data to the model.  Its values won't matter.
> >> Now the two things above will be: proxy_Y[g] will be built into the graph, doing the job of Y[g, 1:T.  For example, proxy_Y[g] will be a dependency of logmu[g, 1:T].  And the way to calculate the log probability will be:
> >> logProb_proxy_Y[g] <- dNBVector(proxy_Y[g], logmu[g,1:T], logphi[g,1:T], g)
> >>
> >> Then you can create dNBVector as follows:
> >> Add it to the list of functions returned from makeRfuns.
> >> Include Y in the keepInR list so dNBVector can access its values by scoping just as calc_log accesses X1, X2, X3.
> >> Use the same steps as you use for calc_log, i.e. dNBVector_internal and then a nimbleRcall called dNBVector.
> >> Notice that if dNBVector takes g as an argument (as shown above), then it can pick out the correct row of Y to use.
> >> dNBVector must take proxy_Y[g] as its first argument, but it can just ignore it.
> >> Have dNBVector return the log probability of all of Y[g, 1:T].  This will be stored as the log probability of proxy_Y[g].
> >>
> >> I hope it makes enough sense to follow!  If I had more time at the moment I would draft it out more fully for you, but let me know if it doesn't work smoothly.
> >>
> >> -Perry

Thanks for reporting on some experimental results.

On Fri, Jul 17, 2020 at 3:29 AM Evgeny Lobzaev <evgeny....@gmail.com> wrote:

> Hi Perry!
>

> Thank you for detailed explanation. I think I understood what needs to be done. I created a code and it works.

> I have few concerns/points to mention.
>  When I declared a proxy_Y node, I had to make it vector-valued(i.e. proxy_Y[g,1:T] instead of suggested proxy_Y[g]). Otherwise, the c++ compilation fails.

This doesn't make sense to me.  In the nimbleRcall prototype are you changing x=double(1) to x=double(0) to tell it the data value will be a scalar?

> I tested 2 instances of the code: one where I keep matrix Y in R and one where I supply matrix Y to nimble. The second case surprisingly runs a bit faster. Is it because of C++ <-> R  data passing overhead or what can be the reason?

It could be the copy overhead.  It could also be the cost of the R evaluator.  In theory things should generally run faster in compiled nimble than in R.  The point of going to R was to avoid scaling problems in nimble.  So, yes and yes, a mix of tradeoffs involved.

> In both versions I had to provide not just a density function for multivariate Negative Binomial distribution (dNBVector) but also a random number generating function (rNBVector). In 2 different situations (provide/not provide Y to nimble) the dNBVector function is coded slightly differently. I wonder if that can contribute to performance issues as well?

Did you mean to say the rNBVector was coded slightly differently?  The "r" function typically isn't used much, unless there are no inits or there are posterior predictive nodes following the distribution.  If the dNBVector is coded differently, yes that could make a difference -- but I think that is self-evident.

> In fact, I will share both versions (that is whether or not Y is supplied to nimble) and, if you have some time/desire, you can take a look.
> I have to say, this is very kind of you and other team members of NIMBLE to help me. You are really helping me with my project and I appreciate that a lot!

Great! Glad to help.  Limited time to dig further into the performance issues right now.  Glad you're up and running.

-Perry

They differ in the MCMC sampling algorithms which are applied to each, automatically, by NIMBLE's MCMC.  Translating your code between these two (mathematically identical) representations is a relatively small and straight-forward exercise.  The relative performance of the different sampling algorithms, as applied to each representation, could differ, would depend on the model and the data, and is generally difficult to predict.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Changing between the stick-breaking representation and the CRP representation, the categorical distribution would persist in your model. On Fri, Jul 17, 2020 at 9:45 AM Perry de Valpine <pdeva...@berkeley.edu> wrote:

> Thanks for reporting on some experimental results.
>
> On Fri, Jul 17, 2020 at 3:29 AM Evgeny Lobzaev <evgeny....@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Hi Perry!
> >
> > Thank you for detailed explanation. I think I understood what needs to be done. I created a code and it works.
> >
> > I have few concerns/points to mention.
> >  When I declared a proxy_Y node, I had to make it vector-valued(i.e. proxy_Y[g,1:T] instead of suggested proxy_Y[g]). Otherwise, the c++ compilation fails.
>
> This doesn't make sense to me.  In the nimbleRcall prototype are you changing x=double(1) to x=double(0) to tell it the data value will be a scalar?
>
> > I tested 2 instances of the code: one where I keep matrix Y in R and one where I supply matrix Y to nimble. The second case surprisingly runs a bit faster. Is it because of C++ <-> R  data passing overhead or what can be the reason?
>
> It could be the copy overhead.  It could also be the cost of the R evaluator.  In theory things should generally run faster in compiled nimble than in R.  The point of going to R was to avoid scaling problems in nimble.  So, yes and yes, a mix of tradeoffs involved.
> > In both versions I had to provide not just a density function for multivariate Negative Binomial distribution (dNBVector) but also a random number generating function (rNBVector). In 2 different situations (provide/not provide Y to nimble) the dNBVector function is coded slightly differently. I wonder if that can contribute to performance issues as well?
> Did you mean to say the rNBVector was coded slightly differently?  The "r" function typically isn't used much, unless there are no inits or there are posterior predictive nodes following the distribution.  If the dNBVector is coded differently, yes that could make a difference -- but I think that is self-evident.
>
> > In fact, I will share both versions (that is whether or not Y is supplied to nimble) and, if you have some time/desire, you can take a look.
> > I have to say, this is very kind of you and other team members of NIMBLE to help me. You are really helping me with my project and I appreciate that a lot!
>
> Great! Glad to help.  Limited time to dig further into the performance issues right now.  Glad you're up and running.
>
> -Perry

> > > A stochastic declaration like
> > > Y[g,1:T] ~ dNBVector(logmu[g,1:T],logphi[g,1:T])    #(I am just using the most recent code in front of me.)
> > > tells nimble that Y[g, 1:T] is a (vector, in this case) stochastic node.  This means two things: Y[g, 1:T] will be built into the graph for determining dependencies among nodes.  And the way to calculate the log probability is:
> > > logProb_Y[g, 1] <- dNBVector(Y[g, 1:T], logmu[g,1:T],logphi[g,1:T])
> > >
> > > So you could do the following:
> > > proxy_Y[g] ~ dNBVector(logmu[g,1:T],logphi[g,1:T], g)
> > > provide proxy_Y[g] as data to the model.  Its values won't matter.
> > > Now the two things above will be: proxy_Y[g] will be built into the graph, doing the job of Y[g, 1:T.  For example, proxy_Y[g] will be a dependency of logmu[g, 1:T].  And the way to calculate the log probability will be:
> > > logProb_proxy_Y[g] <- dNBVector(proxy_Y[g], logmu[g,1:T], logphi[g,1:T], g)
> > >
> > > Then you can create dNBVector as follows:
> > > Add it to the list of functions returned from makeRfuns.
> > > Include Y in the keepInR list so dNBVector can access its values by scoping just as calc_log accesses X1, X2, X3.
> > > Use the same steps as you use for calc_log, i.e. dNBVector_internal and then a nimbleRcall called dNBVector.
> > > Notice that if dNBVector takes g as an argument (as shown above), then it can pick out the correct row of Y to use.
> > > dNBVector must take proxy_Y[g] as its first argument, but it can just ignore it.
> > > Have dNBVector return the log probability of all of Y[g, 1:T].  This will be stored as the log probability of proxy_Y[g].

> > > > > > > I'm not an expert on the BNP facilities offered in NIMBLE, but I think I can comment: the stick-breaking representation (as you're using), and the CRP distribution, are modelling the same Dirichlet process.  They differ in the MCMC sampling algorithms which are applied to each, automatically, by NIMBLE's MCMC.  Translating your code between these two (mathematically identical) representations is a relatively small and straight-forward exercise.  The relative performance of the different sampling algorithms, as applied to each representation, could differ, would depend on the model and the data, and is generally difficult to predict.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Changing between the stick-breaking representation and the CRP representation, the categorical distribution would persist in your model.  And Perry's comments are correct, that (in particular for a large number of categories, e.g. large values of H or HH in your code) the categorical sampler (which is applied to the categorical distribution) would become arbitrarily inefficient, in that it evaluates the posterior density for every category value (H or HH times), then samples directly from that posterior distribution.  And that you could hopefully reduce this inefficiency by writing a customized sampling strategy (a custom-written MCMC sampler), to update your categorical distributions, in a more efficient (less wasteful) manner.

Hi Liz,
Setting useConjugacy=FALSE means you will not get Gibbs samplers.  If you know there is no conjugacy in your model anyway, there is no loss in setting useConjugacy=FALSE.
-Perry

> >
> > If there is any way you can rewrite the temporal part of the model to avoid the long chains of dependencies, you might get better performance anyway.  Sometimes it is possible to rearrange what is stochastic and what is deterministic in a way that reduces the chain of calculations needed for MCMC updates. messages.body_plain:
Hi!

I am trying to use a sparse design matrix in my model, created using the Matrix package. Its class is "dgCMatrix", and it's an S4 object. I'm encountering issues when I attempt to compile the model and mcmc object, getting the below error message:

"Error in storage.mode(values) <- "numeric" : no method for coercing this S4 class to a vector"

Is there a different way to implement sparse matrices in nimble, that will allow for compilation? Or is there a step I should take to coerce the sparse matrix into a different class before compiling?

Thank you in advance for your help!

best,
Liz

messages.subject_clean: compiling sparse matrices (S4 object error)
messages.body_plain:
Currently there is no sparse matrix support built into nimble.  It is on our long-term agenda.

Variables (and nodes) in models must be basic numeric types: vectors, matrices, arrays.  One way you might be able to do it is if there is a way to convert from dgCMatrix to a vector and back.  If you can share more about the use case, we might be able to come up with ideas.

-Perry

messages.body_plain:
Hi Perry,

Thanks for the swift reply - I appreciate your help with this!

I'm working with a design matrix of dimension 33180 x 3472. This matrix captures 3 ecoregion levels I'm working with, so I have 112 dummy variable columns for ecoregion. I then have 30 columns of univariate basis vectors for the covariates I'm interested in. The remaining columns are interaction effects between each ecoregion column and basis vector. 97% of the elements in this matrix are zero entries, which is why I was hoping to use a sparse design matrix in my model.

Not sure if this is relevant/helpful in coming up with a solution, but the model I'm using this matrix in is below:
ZIPcode_icar <- nimbleCode({
  # params for mu and pi calculations
  # i = 2 -> one for mu and one for pi
  for(i in 1:2) {
    alpha[i] ~ dnorm(0,5) # scalar intercept params
    eta[i] ~ dbeta(8,2) # AR param for spatio-temporal adjustments
    sigma_phi[i] ~ dnorm(0,1)  # time difference spatial sd
    beta_param[i] ~ dunif(0,1) # AR param for betas
    tau[i] ~ dnorm(0,5) # precision param
  }

  # AR(1) on betas - for overfitting
  beta_sd <- 0.01
  for(i in 1:2) {
    beta[i,1] ~ dnorm(0, sd = sqrt(beta_sd))
    for(k in 2:p) {
      beta[i,k] ~ dnorm(beta_param[i] * beta[i, k-1], sd = sqrt(beta_sd))
    }
  }

  # spatio-temporal effects
  # IAR prior (spatial)
  for(i in 1:2) {
    phi_sp[1:s, 1, i] ~ dcar_normal(adj = adj[1:L], weights = weights[1:L], num = num[1:s], tau = tau[i])
  }

  # temporal
  for(i in 1:2) {
    phi_full[1:s,1,i] <- phi_sp[1:s, 1, i] * sigma_phi[i]
    for(m in 2:t) {
      phi_full[1:s,m,i] <- eta[i] * phi_full[1:s, m-1, i]  + phi_sp[1:s, 1, i] * sigma_phi[i]
    }
  }

  #likelihood
  for(m in 1:t) {
    for(j in 1:s) {
      log(u[j,m]) <- alpha[1] + inprod(beta[1, 1:p], x[j, 1:p]) + phi_full[j, m, 1] + log_area[j]
      logit(pi_param[j,m]) <- alpha[2] + inprod(beta[2, 1:p], x[j, 1:p]) + phi_full[j,m, 2]
    }
  }

  # vectorize mu and pi
  mu[1:(s*t)] <- nimC(u[1:s,1:t])
  pi[1:(s*t)] <- nimC(pi_param[1:s,1:t])

  for(q in 1:(s*t)) {
    y[q] ~ dZIP(mu[q], zeroProb = pi[q])
  }
})

best,
Liz

Liz, thanks for your interest in nimble.

I've had some success using sparse matrix functions from the Matrix package in nimble.  Specifically, by calling out to Matrix package functions using nimbleRcall.  I maintained the content of the sparse matrices in {row index, column index, value} format, then called out to specifiec sparse matrix functions from the Matrix package.  It took a little bit of setup, but worked in the end.  You can see examples of this in action in the BayesNSGP package, in the fole SGV.R, specifically functions such as R_sparse_tcrossprod, nimble_sparse_tcrossprod, etc:
https://github.com/danielturek/BayesNSGP/blob/master/BayesNSGP/R/SGV.R

These examples might help get you started.

Cheers,
Daniel

On Sat, Jul 18, 2020, 4:15 PM Daniel Turek <db...@williams.edu> wrote:

> Liz, thanks for your interest in nimble.
>
> I've had some success using sparse matrix functions from the Matrix package in nimble.  Specifically, by calling out to Matrix package functions using nimbleRcall.  I maintained the content of the sparse matrices in {row index, column index, value} format, then called out to specifiec sparse matrix functions from the Matrix package.  It took a little bit of setup, but worked in the end.  You can see examples of this in action in the BayesNSGP package, in the fole SGV.R, specifically functions such as R_sparse_tcrossprod, nimble_sparse_tcrossprod, etc:
> https://github.com/danielturek/BayesNSGP/blob/master/BayesNSGP/R/SGV.R
>
> These examples might help get you started.
>
> Cheers,
> Daniel
>
>
> On Sat, Jul 18, 2020 at 5:14 PM Liz Lawler <esla...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Hi Perry,
> >
> > Thanks for the swift reply - I appreciate your help with this!
> >
> > I'm working with a design matrix of dimension 33180 x 3472. This matrix captures 3 ecoregion levels I'm working with, so I have 112 dummy variable columns for ecoregion. I then have 30 columns of univariate basis vectors for the covariates I'm interested in. The remaining columns are interaction effects between each ecoregion column and basis vector. 97% of the elements in this matrix are zero entries, which is why I was hoping to use a sparse design matrix in my model.
> >
> > Not sure if this is relevant/helpful in coming up with a solution, but the model I'm using this matrix in is below:
> > ZIPcode_icar <- nimbleCode({
> >   # params for mu and pi calculations
> >   # i = 2 -> one for mu and one for pi
> >   for(i in 1:2) {
> >     alpha[i] ~ dnorm(0,5) # scalar intercept params
> >     eta[i] ~ dbeta(8,2) # AR param for spatio-temporal adjustments
> >     sigma_phi[i] ~ dnorm(0,1)  # time difference spatial sd
> >     beta_param[i] ~ dunif(0,1) # AR param for betas
> >     tau[i] ~ dnorm(0,5) # precision param
> >   }
> >
> >   # AR(1) on betas - for overfitting
> >   beta_sd <- 0.01
> >   for(i in 1:2) {
> >     beta[i,1] ~ dnorm(0, sd = sqrt(beta_sd))
> >     for(k in 2:p) {
> >       beta[i,k] ~ dnorm(beta_param[i] * beta[i, k-1], sd = sqrt(beta_sd))
> >     }
> >   }
> >
> >   # spatio-temporal effects
> >   # IAR prior (spatial)
> >   for(i in 1:2) {
> >     phi_sp[1:s, 1, i] ~ dcar_normal(adj = adj[1:L], weights = weights[1:L], num = num[1:s], tau = tau[i])
> >   }
> >
> >   # temporal
> >   for(i in 1:2) {
> >     phi_full[1:s,1,i] <- phi_sp[1:s, 1, i] * sigma_phi[i]
> >     for(m in 2:t) {
> >       phi_full[1:s,m,i] <- eta[i] * phi_full[1:s, m-1, i]  + phi_sp[1:s, 1, i] * sigma_phi[i]
> >     }
> >   }
> >
> >   #likelihood
> >   for(m in 1:t) {
> >     for(j in 1:s) {
> >       log(u[j,m]) <- alpha[1] + inprod(beta[1, 1:p], x[j, 1:p]) + phi_full[j, m, 1] + log_area[j]
> >       logit(pi_param[j,m]) <- alpha[2] + inprod(beta[2, 1:p], x[j, 1:p]) + phi_full[j,m, 2]
> >     }
> >   }
> >
> >   # vectorize mu and pi
> >   mu[1:(s*t)] <- nimC(u[1:s,1:t])
> >   pi[1:(s*t)] <- nimC(pi_param[1:s,1:t])
> >
> >   for(q in 1:(s*t)) {
> >     y[q] ~ dZIP(mu[q], zeroProb = pi[q])
> >   }
> > })
> >
> > best,
> > Liz
> >
> >
> >
> > On Saturday, July 18, 2020 at 12:43:51 PM UTC-6, pdevalpine wrote:
> > > Currently there is no sparse matrix support built into nimble.  It is on our long-term agenda.
> > >
> > > Variables (and nodes) in models must be basic numeric types: vectors, matrices, arrays.  One way you might be able to do it is if there is a way to convert from dgCMatrix to a vector and back.  If you can share more about the use case, we might be able to come up with ideas.
> > >
> > > -Perry

messages.body_plain:
Thank you, Daniel! This was a very helpful reference as I played around with the model. I used a combo of yours and Perry's suggestion (from a June 26th thread) and was able to code something up that worked! Did it on a subset of data and am running it on the full dataset now. The code I ended up using is below (highlighted chunks).

Thank you again for your help - I really appreciate it!

best,
Liz

# using all predictors and timesteps (in training set)
s <- 84
t <- as.numeric(dim(sparse_X_eq_tc)[1])/s
p <- as.numeric(dim(sparse_X_eq_tc)[2])

makeRfuns <- function(sparse_matrix) {
  X <- sparse_matrix
  RcalcXB <- function(beta) {
    (X %*% beta)[1:nrow(X),1]
  }
  RcalcXB
}

## source: Perry and Daniel from nimble_users
## Create the functions and put them in .GlobalEnv
RcalcXB_int <- makeRfuns(sparse_X_eq_tc) # needs to be in .GlobalEnv; replace with variable name of sparse matrix

## Define the nimbleRcall nimbleFunctions to call the R function
RcalcXB_model <- nimbleRcall(function(beta = double(1)) {}, returnType = double(1), Rfun = 'RcalcXB_int')

ZIPcode_icar <- nimbleCode({
  # params for mu and pi calculations
  # i = 2 -> one for mu and one for pi
  for(i in 1:2) {
    alpha[i] ~ dnorm(0,5) # scalar intercept params
    eta[i] ~ dbeta(8,2) # AR param for spatio-temporal adjustments
    sigma_phi[i] ~ dnorm(0,1)  # time difference spatial sd
    beta_param[i] ~ dunif(0,1) # AR param for betas
    tau[i] ~ dnorm(0,5) # precision param
  }

  # AR(1) on betas - for overfitting
  beta_sd <- 0.01
  for(i in 1:2) {
    beta[i,1] ~ dnorm(0, sd = sqrt(beta_sd))
    for(k in 2:p) {
      beta[i,k] ~ dnorm(beta_param[i] * beta[i, k-1], sd = sqrt(beta_sd))
    }
  }

  # spatio-temporal effects
  # IAR prior (spatial)
  for(i in 1:2) {
    phi_sp[1:s, 1, i] ~ dcar_normal(adj = adj[1:L], weights = weights[1:L], num = num[1:s], tau = tau[i])
  }

  # temporal
  for(i in 1:2) {
    phi_full[1:s,1,i] <- phi_sp[1:s, 1, i] * sigma_phi[i]
    for(m in 2:t) {
      phi_full[1:s,m,i] <- eta[i] * phi_full[1:s, m-1, i]  + phi_sp[1:s, 1, i] * sigma_phi[i]
    }
  }

  #likelihood params and calculations
  XB[1:(s*t),1] <- RcalcXB_model(beta[1, 1:p])
  XB[1:(s*t),2] <- RcalcXB_model(beta[2, 1:p])

  for(m in 1:t) {
    for(j in 1:s) {

        log(u[j,m]) <- alpha[1] + XB[((m-1) * s + j),1] + phi_full[j, m, 1] + log_area[j]
        logit(pi_param[j,m]) <- alpha[2] + XB[((m-1) * s + j),2] + phi_full[j,m, 2]

    }
  }

  # vectorize mu and pi
  mu[1:(s*t)] <- nimC(u[1:s,1:t])
  pi[1:(s*t)] <- nimC(pi_param[1:s,1:t])

  for(q in 1:(s*t)) {
    y[q] ~ dZIP(mu[q], zeroProb = pi[q])
  }
})

Hello team,

I am working with some data that has a lot of missing values, because of the way sites were sampled. Not every site was surveyed every year, and when a site was surveyed, the number of visits within a year varies. I think I've gotten the indexing correct to deal with the structure of the data, but I was curious about how nimble was treating those missing values. I assumed they would be ignored, but when I monitored the data, it looks like those missing values are being estimated (at least they go from NA to some non NA value). Curious why that might be? In JAGS, when I've done this, those site x year x occasion values have remained missing if I were to monitor the data.

Any insight would be appreciated. Thanks again for creating nimble! Its making it much more efficient to run some of these CAR models!

Cheers,
Paige

messages.body_plain:
Hi Paige,

I'm not connected with the nimble team, but I believe that this is a general Bayesian/MCMC question so I'm going to jump in (and hope that I don't stick my foot in my mouth).

In Bayesian inference you can define the posterior distribution for any collection of random variables (i.e., unknown quantities). A common way to handle missing data in Bayesian inference is to treat missing data in exactly the same way as the observed data by defining the joint pmf/pdf as if these values had been observed. The resulting likelihood function is often referred to as the complete data likelihood since it defines the likelihood (the pmf/pdf as a function of the parameters not the data) as if you had the complete data set in hand.

Using this likelihood you can then construct the posterior distribution for the parameters alone by summing/integrating across the values of the missing data or you can construct the posterior distribution of all the unknown variables, including both the parameters and the the missing data value.

MCMC is simply a method to sample from the posterior distribution defined by the model. If you have missing data for which the pmf/pdf has been defined then samplers will include this variables as part of the posterior distribution and provide samples. You can interpret the distribution formed from these samples as providing information about what the true value would have been if you had observed it. E.g., the posterior median for a missing data values indicates that you believe the truth has a 50-50 chance of being above or below that value.

Without knowing more about your model and your JAGS/nimble code I am more surprised that JAGS didn't provide samples for these values than that nimble did.

I hope that's helpful.

Cheers,

Simon

Thanks for your thoughtful response Simon.

I probably should have provided an example in my first post, my apologies! Below is a snippet of code related to my initial question. The part highlighted in red is my data (counts at each site, each year, on each sampling occasion). The indexing is intended to skip over site x year x occasion combinations where there was no survey, since there is no data there to contribute to the likelihood. I expected that those observations would remain missing, but when I monitor the data, it does seem like they are being updated from NA to some non NA value.

  for(t in 1:nYears){ # 2010-2019
    # Derived parameter - total abundance each year, across study area
    Ntot[t] <- sum(N[1:nSites,t])

    # likelihood
    for(i in 1:nSites){ # loop over grid cells
      # Realized abundance each year and grid cell
      N[i,t] ~ dpois(lambda[i,t])

      # Expected abundance each year and grid cell.
      # Varies as a function of covariate and includes a spatial random effect
      log(lambda[i,t]) <- alpha1*cov[i,t] + rho[i]

    # CAR prior distribution for spatial random effects - 1st order CAR
    rho[1:nSites] ~ dcar_normal(adj[1:L], weights[1:L], num[1:nSites], tauSp, zero_mean=0)
     }

    for(i in 1:nSitesSampled[t]){ # Grid cells surveyed each year
      for(j in 1:nReps[t,i]){ # Number of reps (1 or 2) within each grid cell, each year
        # Count data: Number of birds observed in each grid cell, each year, on each survey
        C[site[t,i],t,j] ~ dbin(p[site[t,i],t,j], N[site[t,i],t])
        Cnew[site[t,i],t,j] ~ dbin(p[site[t,i],t,j], N[site[t,i],t]) # replicate data set

        # Detection probability
        # Intercept varies by vehicle: airplane is the intercept, effect of helicopter is kappa1, and amount of a grid cell covered by each survey (effort)
        logit(p[site[t,i],t,j]) <- kappa0 + kappa1*vehicle[site[t,i],t,j] + kappa2*effort[site[t,i],t,j]
        }}}

Paige, thanks for the question.  Simon, thanks for jumping in.

By coincidence multiple nimble core developers have limited availability this week.

If I follow, your indexing scheme makes sense.  I don't totally follow C vs Cnew.  I'm not sure whether you want both or whether one is a temporary piece of code.  If one of them (Cnew?) is intended for posterior prediction, it would be more efficient if you are able to do that as a separate step, after the MCMC.  I realize that can present logistical hurdles of monitoring what is needed, but the monitors2 and thin2 system may be helpful.  You can use a nimble model for simulation, so you can for example iterate through a sample, use values() <- or nimCopy to put values into a model, and use model$simulate to simulate new values.  This can be done from R for a compiled model or in a nimbleFunction that you can also compile. But anyway that wasn't your question.

On to your question: we will have to look more carefully later to investigate your report of different behavior of JAGS and NIMBLE for NAs interspersed arbitrarily among C[site index, time index, rep index] values.  In the meantime, here are two suggested workarounds.  The first, which will be easier if it works, will be simply to provide non-NA values in those elements of C that are not data.  The only reason to provide NA is to indicate that you want them sampled.  If you provide non-NA values for elements that are not in a declared node (i.e. not declared in the model code), they will (or should) simply be unused.  You could verify that by providing values like -1 that would generate an error if for some reason they are being used when they shouldn't be.  In summary, try replacing your NAs with -1.

The second solution would be to remove samplers from the sampler configuration for the missing data nodes. To do this, you would need to explicitly create your MCMC configuration (as opposed to using nimbleMCMC, for example).  Then you would do something like

Rmodel <- nimbleModel( <your arguments> ) ## with NAs in C to indicate which elements are not data
mcmcConf <- configureMCMC(Rmodel)
# mcmcConf$printSamplers("C") ## do this to see what samplers were assigned, if any, to elements of C and confirm they are for the NA elements
mcmcConf$removeSamplers("C")
# mcmcConf$printSamplers("C") ## do this to verify the result of the previous line

Note that there shouldn't be samplers for data elements of C, so the only samplers would be for non-data elements of C, which are the one you don't want.  If it was more complicated, I would think of tools like Rmodel$isData and Rmodel$expandNodeNames to put together which elements of C are relevant.

Please let us know if one of these ideas works.

-Perry

> > >
> > > I'm not connected with the nimble team, but I believe that this is a general Bayesian/MCMC question so I'm going to jump in (and hope that I don't stick my foot in my mouth).
> > >
> > > In Bayesian inference you can define the posterior distribution for any collection of random variables (i.e., unknown quantities). A common way to handle missing data in Bayesian inference is to treat missing data in exactly the same way as the observed data by defining the joint pmf/pdf as if these values had been observed. The resulting likelihood function is often referred to as the complete data likelihood since it defines the likelihood (the pmf/pdf as a function of the parameters not the data) as if you had the complete data set in hand.
> > >
> > > Using this likelihood you can then construct the posterior distribution for the parameters alone by summing/integrating across the values of the missing data or you can construct the posterior distribution of all the unknown variables, including both the parameters and the the missing data value.
> > >
> > > MCMC is simply a method to sample from the posterior distribution defined by the model. If you have missing data for which the pmf/pdf has been defined then samplers will include this variables as part of the posterior distribution and provide samples. You can interpret the distribution formed from these samples as providing information about what the true value would have been if you had observed it. E.g., the posterior median for a missing data values indicates that you believe the truth has a 50-50 chance of being above or below that value.

I would like to ask if it is possible to configure NIMBLE such that we can call an external simulator within R (using the command system2()), which will return the value used to determine the acceptance of the proposed parameter set that will be used in the MCMC method.

As a starting point, we have now set up some R code to call some external Java code (which we are using as an example for our simulator):

output <- system2("java", args = paste("bbox.Diplomat", runs, prob),

                 stdout = TRUE, stderr = TRUE, stdin = "", input = NULL,

                 env = character(), wait = TRUE, timeout = 0)

where the Java code "bbox.Diplomat" will provide the necessary return value.

If this is possible, we will then look into more details regarding the NIMBLE syntax to set up the procedure (e.g. NIMBLE code, MCMC object). I wonder if there is an option like the example in https://r-nimble.org/examples “Simulating from a model”, but where the data are generated by calling an external simulator.

Thank you in advance, any help will be very much appreciated.

Kind regards,

Ludovica Luisa Vissat

messages.subject: Re: Following adaptation for sampler other than RW
messages.subject_clean: Following adaptation for sampler other than RW
messages.body_plain:
Good question, Rémi.  And I'm glad to hear you found the diagnostic information (scaleHistory, acceptanceRateHistory, etc) in the RW sampler to be helpful.

At present, there's no such facilities in the slice sampler to record this history of the adaption process.  The slice sampler does adapt (every adaptInterval MCMC iterations), to modify the internal "width" variable, to make this "extension" width of the horizontal slice more suitable for the scale of the posterior distribution.  So, yes, tracking this "widthHistory" would be analogous to the adaptation history information in the RW sampler.

At present, this information is not tracked in the slice sampler, but similar methods "getWidthHistory" could be added to the slice sampler.  I don't believe there are plans for adding it at the moment, but we would certainly welcome (and review) a pull-request to add this to the system.

Short of that, modifying the sampler code and/or the nimble code base, you could also track this "width history" by extracting the "width" variable from the slice sampler after each MCMC iteration, making sure to set the nimble option:
nimbleOptions(buildInterfacesForCompiledNestedNimbleFunctions = TRUE)

This would work fine, and accomplish your goals.  A short example showing how to do that is below.

Good luck with this,
Daniel

library(nimble)
nimbleOptions(buildInterfacesForCompiledNestedNimbleFunctions = TRUE)

code <- nimbleCode({
    a ~ dnorm(0, 1)
})
constants <- list()
data <- list()
inits <- list(a = 0)

Rmodel <- nimbleModel(code, constants, data, inits)
Rmodel$calculate()

conf <- configureMCMC(Rmodel, nodes = NULL)
conf$addSampler('a', 'slice')

Rmcmc <- buildMCMC(conf)

Cmodel <- compileNimble(Rmodel)
Cmcmc <- compileNimble(Rmcmc, project = Rmodel)

niter <- 10000
set.seed(0)
widthHistory <- numeric(niter)

for(i in 1:niter) {
    Cmcmc$run(1, reset = (i==1))
    widthHistory[i] <- Cmcmc$samplerFunctions[[1]]$width
}

samples <- as.matrix(Cmcmc$mvSamples)

plot(1:niter, widthHistory, type = 'l')

messages.body_plain:
Hi Rémi,

If you think the RW proposal scale has adapted to a value that is too small, I can give three suggestions for exploring the issue.

1. At the stage of the MCMC configuration (after configureMCMC) but before building the MCMC (before buildMCMC), find the relevant sampler by inspection of mcmcConf$printSamplers() or mcmcConf$getSamplers().  (Here mcmcConf is the object returned by configureMCMC).  Then modify the control list of that sampler to have adapt=FALSE and scale=<your choice>.

2. You can make the same settings by modifying the MCMC (after buildMCMC).  If you do it in the uncompiled version (before compileNimble), you can modify mcmc$samplerFunctions[[idx]]$scale and mcmc$samplerFunctions[[idx]]$adapt, where mcmc is the uncompiled MCMC.  Those values will then be copied to the compiled version to initialize it during compileNimble.  If you want to do it after compileNimble (with say Cmcmc instead of mcmc, where Cmcmc is the compiled version), you will need the same nimbleOptions setting Daniel provided.  You may want to do it this way because you could run it for a while, look at the scale value, then manually adjust it and continue running (with reset = FALSE) to experiment.

3. Sometimes providing good initial values can improve the outcome of the RW adaptation.  If the initial values are far from the main posterior region, then much of the adaptation can occur during updates that are just finding the main posterior region, which can behave very differently that updates in the main region.

HTH
-Perry

messages.subject_clean: NIMBLE and external simulator
messages.body_plain:
Hi Ludovica,

Thanks for your question.  I don't fully follow your use case, but let me try to address your question.

In model code, a node can be deterministic or stochastic.  A stochastic node has a distribution function (a "d" function in standard R distribution notation) and a simulation function (an "r" function in standard R notation).  For MCMC sampling, the "d" function is used to calculate log probabilities for stochastic nodes.  I'm confused because you are asking about calling a simulator (by which we would mean an "r" function) to determine acceptance in MCMC updates (which would typically use a "d" function).  You may be using terms differently.  Can you clarify your use case?   (There are methods, like Particle MCMC, where many simulations are used to obtain an unbiased estimate of an intractable likelihood and that estimate is used for MCMC updating, but that is somewhat specialized.  Please say if you are in any kind of use case like that.)

Either way, here is an outline of how you could connect either a "d" function or an "r" function to your external call.

1. Declare a model node to follow a stochastic declaration that you will define:

output[1:T] ~ dCustom( <parameters> )  ## Automatically calls dCustom for log probability and rCustom for stochastic simulation.

2. Write dCustom and, optionally, rCustom, as nimbleFunctions.  Please see our User Manual Chapter 12: https://r-nimble.org/html_manual/cha-user-defined.html

You only need to provide rCustom if your MCMC (or other method) will need stochastic simulations, which is not usually the case, with the possible exception of initialization if you are not providing inits (which, typically, you should).  You always need to provide dCustom.

3. To have either dCustom and/or rCustom call an R function, create a nimbleRcall for that purpose.  Please see our User Manual section 11.7: https://r-nimble.org/html_manual/cha-RCfunctions.html#sec:calling-R-code

An alternative, if you don't need much else in the model, would be to run the MCMC uncompiled, since the computational overhead might be in your external code anyway.  In that case, you could put the system2 call directly in the nimbleFunction for dCustom and/or rCustom, since they will simply execute in R.

If you need the external call for a deterministic calculation, you can do that in a similar way with a user-defined function rather than a user-defined distribution.

I hope that helps.  As you dig into these layers, let us know further questions.

-Perry

messages.body_plain:
Hi Perry,
Thank you for the suggestion and the explanations to do it, I will give it a try. I am however a bit afraid to fix the RW proposal scale, because it concerns around ~2000 nodes. So I am not sure whether a single (or even a few) scale for all the nodes could do the trick.
I suppose if I manually fix the scale to higher value than produced by the adaptation phase, acceptation rate for those nodes will drop leading to slower iteration through those nodes. Meanwhile the samples should be less autocorrelated and less iterations would be needed ?

Concerning initial values, the model should have relatively good ones for most nodes. I know they have already worked on that and I think that we are currently using older model outputs to initiate the nodes in question. But I will keep that in mind, this could still be problematic.

Best,
Rémi

> Hi Rémi,
>
> If you think the RW proposal scale has adapted to a value that is too small, I can give three suggestions for exploring the issue.
>
> 1. At the stage of the MCMC configuration (after configureMCMC) but before building the MCMC (before buildMCMC), find the relevant sampler by inspection of mcmcConf$printSamplers() or mcmcConf$getSamplers().  (Here mcmcConf is the object returned by configureMCMC).  Then modify the control list of that sampler to have adapt=FALSE and scale=<your choice>.
>
> 2. You can make the same settings by modifying the MCMC (after buildMCMC).  If you do it in the uncompiled version (before compileNimble), you can modify mcmc$samplerFunctions[[idx]]$scale and mcmc$samplerFunctions[[idx]]$adapt, where mcmc is the uncompiled MCMC.  Those values will then be copied to the compiled version to initialize it during compileNimble.  If you want to do it after compileNimble (with say Cmcmc instead of mcmc, where Cmcmc is the compiled version), you will need the same nimbleOptions setting Daniel provided.  You may want to do it this way because you could run it for a while, look at the scale value, then manually adjust it and continue running (with reset = FALSE) to experiment.
>
> 3. Sometimes providing good initial values can improve the outcome of the RW adaptation.  If the initial values are far from the main posterior region, then much of the adaptation can occur during updates that are just finding the main posterior region, which can behave very differently that updates in the main region.

> HTH
> -Perry

Hi Rémi,

Sure that makes sense.  You could write a for loop to iterate over samplers for many nodes to set the proposal scale and turn the adapt flag FALSE for each one.  I suggested it because it sounded like you were conjecturing that the adaptation has not resulted in proposal scales that you think are most efficient.  (We usually think of efficiency in terms of (effective sample size) / computation time.  The computation time shouldn't change much or at all for different proposal scales, but the effective sample sizes almost certainly will.)  That is possible.  If you increase proposal scale, it may or may not increase effective sample size.  If it does, then fewer iterations would be needed.  I hope that helps.  Let us know if you get interesting results.

-Perry

> > > > > > > > I'm not an expert on the BNP facilities offered in NIMBLE, but I think I can comment: the stick-breaking representation (as you're using), and the CRP distribution, are modelling the same Dirichlet process.  They differ in the MCMC sampling algorithms which are applied to each, automatically, by NIMBLE's MCMC.  Translating your code between these two (mathematically identical) representations is a relatively small and straight-forward exercise.  The relative performance of the different sampling algorithms, as applied to each representation, could differ, would depend on the model and the data, and is generally difficult to predict.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > Changing between the stick-breaking representation and the CRP representation, the categorical distribution would persist in your model.  And Perry's comments are correct, that (in particular for a large number of categories, e.g. large values of H or HH in your code) the categorical sampler (which is applied to the categorical distribution) would become arbitrarily inefficient, in that it evaluates the posterior density for every category value (H or HH times), then samples directly from that posterior distribution. > > > > > > > > > > Looking at your model, I wonder if the following would work: Vectorize logmu and logphi over t (since any change in a parameter will affect all t).  And use a vector of dummy data values to push calculation of phi[g, 1:T], p[g, 1:T] and log probabilities of y[g, 1:T] to R (or C++) using the trick I showed in the June 26 message.  Your model code would have something like:
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > dummy[g] ~ dCustom(logmu[g, 1:T],  logphi[g, 1:T], g ) # do the phi, p and y steps all together

> > > > > > > > > >

> > > > > > > > > >

> > > > > > > > > >

> > > > > > > > > >

> > > > > > > > > >

> > > > > > > > > >

> > > > > > > > > I'm not an expert on the BNP facilities offered in NIMBLE, but I think I can comment: the stick-breaking representation (as you're using), and the CRP distribution, are modelling the same Dirichlet process.  They differ in the MCMC sampling algorithms which are applied to each, automatically, by NIMBLE's MCMC.  Translating your code between these two (mathematically identical) representations is a relatively small and straight-forward exercise.  The relative performance of the different sampling algorithms, as applied to each representation, could differ, would depend on the model and the data, and is generally difficult to predict.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > Changing between the stick-breaking representation and the CRP representation, the categorical distribution would persist in your model.  And Perry's comments are correct, that (in particular for a large number of categories, e.g. large values of H or HH in your code) the categorical sampler (which is applied to the categorical distribution) would become arbitrarily inefficient, in that it evaluates the posterior density for every category value (H or HH times), then samples directly from that posterior distribution.  And that you could hopefully reduce this inefficiency by writing a customized sampling strategy (a custom-written MCMC sampler), to update your categorical distributions, in a more efficient (less wasteful) manner.
